title: Foundations
subtitle: The people, the Torah, faith and history
intro: Who is a Jew and what is giyur, the Written and the Oral Torah, the principles of faith, the covenant, the history of the people, the mitzvot and the movements of Judaism — the foundation of the whole course.

overview.why: This section is the foundation of the whole course: who is a Jew and what is giyur, the Written and the Oral Torah, faith in the one G-d and the covenant, the history of the people, the mitzvot and the movements. Here you build an understanding of what a ger is entering and to whom they are coming: without these foundations it is impossible to enter Judaism consciously. Every following topic — Shabbat, kashrut, the festivals — rests on this layer.
overview.examFocus: At the beit din you are usually asked about your personal motivation (“why do you want giyur?”), about the foundations of faith and the unity of G-d, about the candidate's place in the Jewish people and its history, about the Land of Israel, about the mitzvot and the movement you have chosen. Be ready to answer in your own words: about the Shema, the 13 principles, the Mashiach who is still awaited, the eternal Torah, and how you read the Tanakh together with your community. A good answer is sincere and specific.
goals: Explain who a Jew is and what giyur is in essence, drawing on Ruth and the Talmud
Describe the structure of the Tanakh, the Oral Torah, the Mishnah and the Talmud
Name the Rambam's 13 principles of faith, explain them in your own words, and understand what Judaism expects of the Mashiach
Understand the Shema and the indivisible unity of G-d, the covenant, and chosenness as responsibility
Find your way in the history of the people, its bond with the Land of Israel, the 613 mitzvot and the movements of Judaism

lessons.title: Who is a Jew and what is giyur
citations: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Forbidden Relations 13:1–4; 14:1–5
keyIdeas: Jews are not a race but the covenant people of the descendants of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, who received the Torah at Sinai; one can join it through giyur.
According to traditional halacha, a Jew is someone born to a Jewish mother or who has undergone giyur; not observing the mitzvot does not cancel this.
Ruth's words “your people are my people, and your G-d is my G-d” are the formula of giyur: first the people, then faith and the mitzvot.
Giyur according to halacha: kabbalat ol mitzvot before a beit din, brit milah or hatafat dam brit, tevilah in a mikveh; in Progressive communities the rabbi determines the rites.
Orthodox giyur is recognized by all; Masorti giyur by Reform and Conservative, not by Orthodoxy; Reform giyur by Reform (and by Masorti if brit milah and tevilah took place).

blocks.text: A people you can join

Jews are not a race, nor simply a nationality in the modern sense. The Jewish people is a *covenant people*: the family of the descendants of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, which took the Torah upon itself at Mount Sinai. That is exactly why it is possible to join this people. A person cannot become “of other blood”, but can enter the covenant – and then becomes a Jew fully, without reservation. This path is called **giyur**, and a person who has gone through it is a **ger** (feminine – **giyoret**).

According to traditional halacha, a Jew is someone born to a Jewish mother or someone who has undergone giyur. Jewishness is passed down through the mother: the Talmud derives this principle from the verses of Devarim (Deuteronomy) 7:3–4 (Kiddushin 68b). A Jewish father with a non-Jewish mother does not, according to halacha, pass Jewishness on to the child – which is why many people from mixed families of the former USSR, who grew up with a Jewish surname and a Jewish sense of self, come specifically to giyur.

Important: a Jew does not stop being a Jew even if he does not observe the mitzvot. The Talmud says: “Israel, even though it has sinned, is still Israel” (Sanhedrin 44a). Jewishness is not a club membership that can be cancelled, but belonging to a people. In the same way, a ger after giyur remains a Jew forever.

Since 1983 (a resolution of the Central Conference of American Rabbis, CCAR), **Reform Judaism** in the USA has recognized as Jewish the child of *either* Jewish parent – father or mother – if the child is raised with a Jewish identity and this is confirmed by public acts (naming, Jewish education, bar or bat mitzvah). This is called the principle of “patrilineal descent”. Conservative (Masorti) and Orthodox Judaism do not accept this principle.

differs.text: Masorti, like Orthodoxy, recognizes Jewishness only through the mother or through giyur; the child of a Jewish father and a non-Jewish mother needs giyur.

blocks.text: Ruth – the model of a giyoret

The best-known example of giyur in the Tanakh is Ruth the Moabite. After her husband's death, her mother-in-law Naomi urged her to return to her own people, but Ruth answered with words that became the formula of every giyur:

blocks.he: כִּי אֶל אֲשֶׁר תֵּלְכִי אֵלֵךְ, וּבַאֲשֶׁר תָּלִינִי אָלִין; עַמֵּךְ עַמִּי, וֵאלֹהַיִךְ אֱלֹהָי
blocks.translit: Ki el asher telchi elech, u-va'asher talini alin; amech ami, ve'Elohayich Elohai
blocks.ru: Wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you lodge, I will lodge; your people are my people, and your G-d is my G-d

blocks.text: Notice the order: first “your people are my people”, and only then “your G-d is my G-d”. Giyur is at once joining the *people*, with its destiny and history, and accepting *the faith and the mitzvot*. One without the other is incomplete. Ruth became the great-grandmother of King David (Ruth 4:17), and therefore, according to tradition, an ancestor of the Mashiach. Her book is read on the festival of Shavuot – the day of the giving of the Torah, because at Sinai, in the words of the Sages, the whole people itself “underwent giyur”.
How giyur is performed according to halacha
The Talmud (Yevamot 46a–47b) and the Rambam (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Forbidden Relations, ch. 13–14) describe giyur the way our ancestors underwent it at Sinai. It includes:

items: **Kabbalat ol mitzvot** – taking upon oneself the “yoke of the mitzvot”, that is, the commitment to observe the Torah, before a beit din.
**Brit milah** – circumcision for a man; if the man is already circumcised, a symbolic drawing of a drop of blood is performed – *hatafat dam brit*.
**Tevilah** – immersion in a mikveh (ritual pool) in the presence of the beit din; for a woman this is the main rite of giyur.
In the time of the Temple, a sacrifice (korban) was also added; today there is none.

differs.text: Historically, Reform Judaism (CCAR resolution of 1892) did not require either circumcision or the mikveh. Today many Progressive communities, including in Israel and the CIS countries, perform both tevilah and brit milah, but the decision is made by the community's rabbi.

blocks.text: Giyur is performed before a **beit din** – a rabbinical court of three. According to the Rambam, the beit din first asks the candidate: “What have you seen that you have come to convert? Do you not know that the people of Israel in our time are oppressed and persecuted?” If the person answers: “I know, and I am not worthy of it,” he is accepted and taught the foundations of the faith and some of the lighter and weightier mitzvot (Yevamot 47a; Laws of Forbidden Relations 14:1–2). Hence the custom of at first discouraging the candidate: not in order to push him away, but so that the decision is free and serious.

Orthodox halacha requires accepting *all* the mitzvot: a candidate who declares in advance that he will accept the Torah except for one mitzvah is not accepted (Bechorot 30b). That is why an Orthodox beit din checks not only knowledge but also real life: keeping Shabbat, kashrut, the laws of family purity, and connection with a community.

“righteous convert” – a person who has undergone full giyur and become a Jew in every respect. In contrast, a *ger toshav* (גֵּר תּוֹשָׁב) – “resident stranger” – is a non-Jew who has accepted the seven laws of the descendants of Noach but has not become a Jew.
The ger's place among the people

The Sages say: “A ger who has converted is like a newborn child” (Yevamot 22a). He begins a new life, receives a Hebrew name and is called the son or daughter of our father Avraham and our mother Sarah – for example, “Rut bat Avraham Avinu ve-Sarah Imenu”. The past does not become a disgrace: the Torah repeatedly commands us to love the ger and forbids reminding him of his origins.

blocks.he: וַאֲהַבְתֶּם אֶת הַגֵּר, כִּי גֵרִים הֱיִיתֶם בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם
blocks.translit: Va'ahavtem et ha-ger, ki gerim heyitem be'eretz Mitzrayim
blocks.ru: Love the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt

blocks.text: The prohibition against wronging a ger – by word or deed – is written explicitly in the Torah (Shemot 22:20; Vayikra 19:33–34). The Talmud notes that the Torah warns about the ger many times – according to one opinion, thirty-six times (Bava Metzia 59b). One of the greatest Sages, Hillel, accepted for giyur a man who came to him with the brazen request to “teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot”, and answered: “What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow – that is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary; go and learn” (Shabbat 31a). According to tradition, great teachers also descended from gerim – Shemaya and Avtalyon, and Rabbi Akiva was a descendant of gerim.
Recognition of conversions today
Today giyur is performed by batei din of different movements, and it is important to understand honestly who recognizes which conversions:

items: **Orthodox** giyur is recognized by all movements. In Israel, registering a marriage through the Chief Rabbinate requires an Orthodox giyur recognized by the Rabbinate itself.
**Conservative (Masorti)** giyur is recognized by Conservative and Reform communities; Orthodoxy does not recognize it.
**Reform (Progressive)** giyur is recognized by Reform communities; recognition by Conservative communities depends on whether brit milah and tevilah were performed; Orthodoxy does not recognize it.

For the right to make aliyah to Israel under the Law of Return, the state recognizes conversions performed in recognized Jewish communities abroad, including non-Orthodox ones; in 2021 the Supreme Court of Israel extended this to non-Orthodox conversions performed in Israel itself.

blocks.text: Before choosing a path, ask yourself honestly which community you want to live in, where your children will study and where you plan to marry. The rabbi of your giyur program will explain in detail how his particular beit din is recognized.

Whichever path you choose, the essence is the same: giyur is not a formality or a “change of passport”, but a decision to bind your life and the life of your future children to the Jewish people and its covenant with the Almighty. As Ruth said: “your people are my people, and your G-d is my G-d.”

lessons.title: The Written and the Oral Torah
keyIdeas: “Torah” means teaching and instruction: in the narrow sense, the Five Books of Moses; in the broad sense, all Jewish teaching, from the Tanakh to the works of the rabbis.
The Tanakh is Torah (5), Nevi'im (8) and Ketuvim (11), 24 books in all; a sefer Torah is written by hand and read through in the synagogue over a year.
The Oral Torah is the interpretation given to Moshe at Sinai together with the Written Torah; without it one cannot fulfill tefillin or shechitah, nor know what is forbidden on Shabbat.
The Mishnah was compiled around 200 CE by Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi; the Mishnah and the Gemara make up the Talmud: the Yerushalmi and the Babylonian.
The codes brought the Talmud down to practice: the Rambam's Mishneh Torah, the Shulchan Aruch with the Rema's Ashkenazi Mappah, the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch.

blocks.text: What the word “Torah” means

The word **Torah** (תּוֹרָה) comes from a root meaning “to point out, to instruct” – it is not so much “law” as *teaching*, showing the way. In the narrow sense, the Torah is the Five Books of Moses, the five books written down, according to tradition, by Moshe (Moses) from the words of the Almighty. In the broad sense, all Jewish religious teaching is called Torah – from the Tanakh to the works of contemporary rabbis.

blocks.he: תּוֹרָה צִוָּה לָנוּ מֹשֶׁה, מוֹרָשָׁה קְהִלַּת יַעֲקֹב
blocks.translit: Torah tzivah lanu Moshe, morashah kehillat Yaakov
blocks.ru: Moshe commanded us the Torah – the heritage of the congregation of Yaakov

blocks.text: Traditionally, this is one of the first verses a small child in a Jewish family learns. The Torah is the *heritage* of the whole community, not the property of rabbis or scholars: every Jew, including a ger, receives it in full.
The Tanakh: 24 books

The Holy Scriptures of the Jewish people are called the **Tanakh** – an acronym of the first letters of its three parts: **T**orah, **N**evi'im (Prophets), **K**etuvim (Writings). By the Jewish count the Tanakh has 24 books (already the Talmud counts them this way, Bava Batra 14b). In editions that divide the same texts differently there are more books, because some of them are split into two parts, and the order of the books is different.

items: **Torah (5 books):** Bereshit (Genesis), Shemot (Exodus), Vayikra (Leviticus), Bamidbar (Numbers), Devarim (Deuteronomy).

**Nevi'im (8 books):** Yehoshua, Shoftim (Judges), Shmuel (Samuel, one book), Melachim (Kings, one book), Yeshayahu (Isaiah), Yirmiyahu (Jeremiah), Yechezkel (Ezekiel) and Trei Asar – “The Twelve” minor prophets, counted as one book.

**Ketuvim (11 books):** Tehillim (Psalms), Mishlei (Proverbs), Iyov (Job), Shir HaShirim (Song of Songs), Ruth, Eichah (Lamentations), Kohelet (Ecclesiastes), Esther, Daniel, Ezra-Nechemiah (one book), Divrei HaYamim (Chronicles, one book).

blocks.text: In total, 5 + 8 + 11 = 24. Five books of the Ketuvim – Shir HaShirim, Ruth, Eichah, Kohelet and Esther – are called the **five megillot** (“scrolls”); each is read on a particular day of the year: the Song of Songs on Pesach, Ruth on Shavuot, Eichah on the 9th of Av, Kohelet on Sukkot, Esther on Purim.

Why do we say “Tanakh” rather than calling it an “old”, that is, outdated, covenant? Such a name implies that the covenant of Sinai has supposedly grown old and been replaced by another. Judaism does not accept this. The Torah calls the covenant with Israel eternal – *brit olam* (as is said of the covenant of Avraham, Bereshit 17:7, and of Shabbat, Shemot 31:16), and Moshe says that he makes it “not with you alone… but also with those who are not here with us today” (Devarim 29:13–14), that is, with all generations. The covenant of Sinai is not “old” and not the first of two: it is one, eternal and unchanging (Rambam, 9th principle; Foundations of the Torah 9:1). And the text of the Torah has been copied letter for letter for thousands of years, as mentioned above regarding the sefer Torah.

The Torah for reading in the synagogue is written by hand on parchment – this is a **sefer Torah**, a scroll written by a specially trained scribe, a *sofer*. A single error in one letter makes the scroll unfit until it is corrected. The Torah is divided into 54 weekly portions (*the weekly parashah*, *parashat ha-shavua*), and over the course of a year it is read in full in the synagogue; the cycle ends and begins anew on the festival of Simchat Torah.
Why the Oral Torah is needed

Judaism teaches that at Sinai Moshe received not only the written text but also its interpretation – the **Oral Torah** (*Torah she-be'al peh*). Without it, many mitzvot of the Written Torah simply cannot be fulfilled. A few examples:

items: The Torah commands: “bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be *totafot* between your eyes” (Devarim 6:8). What are totafot, what are they made of, and how? The answer – tefillin, black leather boxes with straps – is given in the Oral Torah.

The Torah permits meat: “and you shall slaughter… as I have commanded you” (Devarim 12:21) – but nowhere in the Written Torah is it described *how* exactly one is commanded to slaughter. The laws of shechitah were passed down orally.
The Torah forbids “any work” on Shabbat (Shemot 20:10) but does not define what work is. The list of 39 categories of creative work (melachot) is found in the Mishnah (Shabbat 7:2).

blocks.text: The Torah was given forever: “Everything I command you, take care to do it; do not add to it and do not take away from it” (Devarim 13:1). The Rambam derives from this that no prophet can annul a commandment of the Torah (Foundations of the Torah 9:1; the 9th principle). Therefore he calls the claim that the commandments have been replaced by another, “new” covenant a denial of the Torah (Laws of Teshuvah 3:8). Sometimes people cite the words of Yirmiyahu that the Almighty will make “a new covenant” with the house of Israel (Yirmiyahu 31:30–32). But the same passage says what it consists of: “I will put My Torah within them and write it on their hearts.” It speaks of the same Torah, which the people will know by heart, not of its abolition.
At the beginning of tractate Avot, the Mishnah describes the chain through which this teaching was passed down:

blocks.he: מֹשֶׁה קִבֵּל תּוֹרָה מִסִּינַי, וּמְסָרָהּ לִיהוֹשֻׁעַ, וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ לִזְקֵנִים, וּזְקֵנִים לִנְבִיאִים, וּנְבִיאִים מְסָרוּהָ לְאַנְשֵׁי כְנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה
blocks.translit: Moshe kibel Torah miSinai, umsarah liYehoshua, viYehoshua lizkenim, uzkenim linvi'im, unvi'im mesaruha le'anshei Knesset HaGedolah
blocks.ru: Moshe received the Torah from Sinai and passed it on to Yehoshua, Yehoshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets passed it on to the Men of the Great Assembly

blocks.text: In Second Temple times, disputes over the Oral Torah divided the people: the *Pharisees* (Perushim), from whom all of rabbinic Judaism descends, accepted it, while the *Sadducees* (Tzedukim) recognized only the Written Torah. Later, from the 8th century, the Oral Torah was also rejected by the *Karaites*.

People sometimes say: “The written text itself is enough for us; we can do without the interpretations of the sages.” But it was precisely the sages who preserved how to fulfill the commandments of the Written Torah. A path that discards the Oral Torah while still using a kippah, Shabbat candles or the word “rabbi” contradicts itself: these very customs come from the tradition of the sages. The Torah is read together with the people who lived it, not against them.
Mishnah and Talmud

For a long time it was forbidden to write down the Oral Torah. But after the destruction of the Second Temple (70 CE) and the persecutions that followed, there was a danger that the teaching would be forgotten. Around 200 CE **Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi** (“the Prince”) gathered the oral laws into a single book — the **Mishnah**. It is written in Hebrew and divided into six orders (*sedarim*), which is why the whole Talmud is called by the abbreviation **Shas** (shishah sedarim — “six orders”):

items: Zera'im (“Seeds”) — blessings and agricultural laws;
Mo'ed (“Appointed Time”) — Shabbat and the festivals;
Nashim (“Women”) — marriage and divorce;
Nezikin (“Damages”) — civil and criminal law, as well as tractate Avot;
Kodashim (“Holy Things”) — the Temple, sacrifices, shechitah;
Taharot (“Purity”) — the laws of ritual purity.

blocks.text: The sages of the Mishnah era are called *tannaim*. The following generations of scholars — the *amoraim* — in the Land of Israel and in Babylonia discussed and interpreted the Mishnah; these discussions, recorded in Aramaic and Hebrew, are called the **Gemara**. The Mishnah together with the Gemara is the **Talmud**. There are two Talmuds: the Jerusalem Talmud (*Yerushalmi*, completed around 400) and the larger and more authoritative Babylonian Talmud (*Bavli*, completed around 500). Alongside the Talmud there are the **midrashim** — interpretations of the text of the Tanakh, both legal and narrative (aggadah).
Halacha and the great codes
Jewish law; from the root “to walk” — literally “the way in which one walks.” Halacha embraces all of life: prayer, food, Shabbat, family, commerce, the courts.

Since the Talmud is a record of debates rather than a ready-made set of rules, codes appeared later. The **Rambam** (Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon, Maimonides, 1138–1204) wrote the “Mishneh Torah” — a code of all of halacha in 14 books, in clear Hebrew. In the 16th century **Rabbi Yosef Karo** compiled the **Shulchan Aruch** (“The Set Table”), first printed in Venice in 1565. It is divided into four parts: *Orach Chaim* (prayer, Shabbat, festivals), *Yoreh De'ah* (kashrut, mourning, etc.), *Even HaEzer* (marriage) and *Choshen Mishpat* (civil law). The Shulchan Aruch largely follows Sephardi custom, and **Rabbi Moshe Isserles** (the Rema) of Kraków added glosses to it — the “Mappah” (“The Tablecloth”) with Ashkenazi customs. That is why to this day Sephardim and Ashkenazim act differently on a number of questions.

In 1864 Rabbi Shlomo Ganzfried published a short practical code — the **Kitzur Shulchan Aruch**, which beginners still often study today (including in Russian translation). Halachic authorities are divided into the *rishonim* (“the first ones,” roughly 11th–15th centuries) and the *acharonim* (“the later ones,” after the Shulchan Aruch).

The movements of Judaism understand the nature of these texts differently. Orthodoxy regards the Written and Oral Torah as divine revelation and halacha as binding. Conservative Judaism recognizes halacha as binding but sees it as a historically developing system. Reform Judaism sees the Torah and the Talmud as an inspired, yet humanly created, heritage from which each person consciously chooses their practice.

differs.text: Reform Judaism does not consider halacha binding as a whole: the ethical commandments are the foundation, while ritual ones are observed by informed personal and communal choice.

cards.front: What does the word “Torah” literally mean?
cards.back: Teaching, instruction, showing the way.

cards.front: What does the abbreviation “Tanakh” stand for?
cards.back: Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets), Ketuvim (Writings).

cards.front: How many books are in the Tanakh by the Jewish count?
cards.back: 24: Torah — 5, Nevi'im — 8, Ketuvim — 11.

cards.front: Name the five books of the Torah.
cards.back: Bereshit, Shemot, Vayikra, Bamidbar, Devarim.

cards.front: What is “Trei Asar”?
cards.back: The book of the twelve minor prophets, counted in the Tanakh as a single book.

cards.front: Name the five megillot.
cards.back: Shir HaShirim, Ruth, Eichah, Kohelet, Esther.

cards.front: Into how many weekly portions is the Torah divided?
cards.back: Into 54; the annual cycle concludes on Simchat Torah.

cards.front: What is the Oral Torah?
cards.back: The interpretation and laws given at Sinai together with the Written Torah; later written down in the Mishnah and Talmud.

cards.front: Give an example of why the Oral Torah is needed.
cards.back: Tefillin (“totafot,” Devarim 6:8), shechitah (Devarim 12:21), the 39 categories of work on Shabbat — the details are found only in the Oral Torah.

cards.front: To whom did Moshe pass on the Torah (Avot 1:1)?
cards.back: To Yehoshua; then to the elders, the prophets and the Men of the Great Assembly.

cards.front: Who compiled the Mishnah, and when?
cards.back: Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, around 200 CE.

cards.front: What is “Shas”?
cards.back: “Shishah sedarim” — the six orders of the Mishnah; the name is used for the whole Talmud.

cards.front: Talmud = ?
cards.back: Mishnah + Gemara. There is the Jerusalem Talmud (c. 400) and the Babylonian Talmud (c. 500).

cards.front: What does the word “halacha” mean?
cards.back: Jewish law; from the root “to walk” — “the way.”

cards.front: What is the Rambam's code called?
cards.back: The “Mishneh Torah” — a code of all of halacha in 14 books.

cards.front: Who compiled the Shulchan Aruch, and who added the Ashkenazi glosses?
cards.back: Rabbi Yosef Karo (published 1565); the “Mappah” glosses — Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema).

cards.front: Which groups rejected the Oral Torah?
cards.back: The Sadducees (Second Temple era) and the Karaites (from the 8th century).

cards.front: In what languages are the Mishnah and Gemara written?
cards.back: The Mishnah — in Hebrew; the Gemara — in Aramaic and Hebrew.

cards.front: What are midrashim?
cards.back: Interpretations of the text of the Tanakh — legal and narrative (aggadah).

cards.front: What is parashat hashavua?
cards.back: The weekly Torah portion; the whole annual cycle (54 portions) concludes on Simchat Torah.

cards.front: Where and when was the Shulchan Aruch first printed?
cards.back: In Venice in 1565.

cards.front: Name the four parts of the Shulchan Aruch.
cards.back: Orach Chaim, Yoreh De'ah, Even HaEzer, Choshen Mishpat.

cards.front: Why do Ashkenazim and Sephardim act differently on a number of questions?
cards.back: The Shulchan Aruch follows Sephardi custom, while the Rema's Mappah records Ashkenazi custom.

cards.front: How does Reform Judaism understand the Torah and the Talmud?
cards.back: The Torah and the Talmud are an inspired, yet humanly created, heritage; practice is chosen from it consciously.

cards.front: Can the commandments of the Torah be annulled or replaced?
cards.back: No: “do not add and do not take away” (Devarim 13:1). No prophet can annul them (Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 9:1). The teaching that the Torah has been replaced is a false teaching.

cards.front: What is Yirmiyahu 31:30–32, which mentions “a new covenant,” speaking about?
cards.back: “I will put My Torah within them and write it on their hearts”: it speaks of the same Torah, which the people will know by heart, not of its abolition.

cards.front: Why do we say “Tanakh” rather than calling it an “old” (outdated) covenant?
cards.back: Such a name implies that the covenant of Sinai has been replaced by another. For Judaism the covenant of Sinai is eternal (Devarim 29:13–14), and there is no other covenant to replace it.

cards.front: With whom was the covenant at Sinai made, according to Devarim 29:13–14?
cards.back: Not only with those who stood there, but also “with those who are not here with us today” — with all future generations.

cards.front: Can one live by the Torah while bypassing the Oral Torah and the sages?
cards.back: No. Without the Oral Torah, it is unknown how to fulfill the commandments. “Only the written lines” is not the way of Judaism.

lessons.title: The Rambam's Thirteen Principles of Faith
citations: Rambam, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin, ch. 10 (Perek Chelek)
keyIdeas: In his commentary on the Mishnah (Sanhedrin ch. 10, “Perek Chelek”), the Rambam formulated the 13 principles of faith.
Groups of principles: 1–5 — about G-d, 6–9 — about prophecy and the Torah, 10–13 — about Divine providence and the future.
The prose form of the principles is “Ani Ma'amin” in the siddur; the poetic form is the hymn “Yigdal.”
According to testimonies, Jews in the ghettos and death camps sang the words of “Ani Ma'amin” about the coming of Mashiach.
Crescas, Albo and Abarbanel built the foundations differently; the movements understand the principles differently, especially 8–9 and 12–13.

blocks.text: Judaism — faith or action?

Judaism is often called a “religion of deeds”: what matters most is not what a person thinks but how they live. The Tanakh contains no formal creed, and the Torah commands concrete actions. And yet Jewish life does have a foundation of belief. The Mishnah says: “All Israel have a share in the World to Come,” — and immediately lists those who lose it, for example those who deny that the Torah is from Heaven (Sanhedrin 10:1). Commenting on this mishnah (the chapter known as “Perek Chelek”), the **Rambam** (1138–1204) was the first to formulate a systematic list of the foundations of faith — the **13 principles** (*ikkarim*).
The Thirteen Principles

items: **The existence of the Creator.** G-d exists; He created everything and governs all that has been created.
**Unity.** G-d is One; His unity is unlike any other; there are no other gods.
**Incorporeality.** G-d has no body or form, and the properties of matter do not apply to Him.
**Eternity.** G-d is the first and the last: He existed before everything and will endure forever.
**Prayer to G-d alone.** One may pray only to Him; one may not turn to intermediaries — angels, heavenly bodies, people.
**Prophecy.** G-d reveals His will to people through prophets.
**The prophecy of Moshe.** Moshe is the greatest of the prophets, both before and after him.
**The Torah is from Heaven.** The entire Torah that we have was given to Moshe.
**The immutability of the Torah.** This Torah will not be replaced, and there will be no other Torah from the Creator.
**Omniscience.** G-d knows all the deeds and thoughts of people.
**Reward and punishment.** G-d rewards those who keep the commandments and punishes those who transgress them.
**The coming of Mashiach.** Mashiach will come; even though he tarries, one must await him every day.
**The resurrection of the dead** (*techiyat hametim*) — will take place when the Creator wills it.

blocks.text: The principles are easy to remember in groups. The first five speak about *G-d*: He exists, He is One, incorporeal, eternal, and He alone is to be served. Principles 6–9 speak about *the Torah and prophecy*: G-d speaks with people, the highest revelation came through Moshe, the Torah is from G-d and unchanging. The last four are about *Divine providence and the future*: G-d knows, judges, will bring Mashiach and will resurrect the dead.

The Rambam writes that whoever denies even one of these foundations leaves the community of Israel (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin ch. 10). This makes it clear why Judaism regards as false teachings, for example, the doctrine of G-d in several persons (contrary to the 2nd and 3rd principles), prayer through an intermediary (contrary to the 5th), and the belief that Mashiach has already come and will return (contrary to the 12th) (Rambam, Laws of Teshuvah 3:6–7; Laws of Kings 11:4).
“Ani Ma'amin” — “I believe”

Many siddurim print a short prose form of the 13 principles after the morning prayer. Each one begins with the words *“Ani ma'amin be'emunah shleimah”* — “I believe with complete faith.” The author of this text is unknown; it is based on the Rambam's formulations. Here is the first principle:

blocks.he: אֲנִי מַאֲמִין בֶּאֱמוּנָה שְׁלֵמָה, שֶׁהַבּוֹרֵא יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ הוּא בּוֹרֵא וּמַנְהִיג לְכָל הַבְּרוּאִים, וְהוּא לְבַדּוֹ עָשָׂה וְעוֹשֶׂה וְיַעֲשֶׂה לְכָל הַמַּעֲשִׂים
blocks.translit: Ani ma'amin be'emunah shleimah, shehaBorei yitbarach shemo hu borei umanhig lechol habru'im, vehu levado asah ve'oseh veya'aseh lechol hama'asim
blocks.ru: I believe with complete faith that the Creator, blessed be His name, is the Maker and Ruler of all creatures, and that He alone made, makes and will make all things

blocks.text: And here is the twelfth principle — about Mashiach. According to testimonies, these words, set to music, were sung by Jews in the ghettos and death camps during the Shoah; for many they became a hymn of faith in spite of everything:

blocks.he: אֲנִי מַאֲמִין בֶּאֱמוּנָה שְׁלֵמָה בְּבִיאַת הַמָּשִׁיחַ, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיִּתְמַהְמֵהַּ, עִם כָּל זֶה אֲחַכֶּה לּוֹ בְּכָל יוֹם שֶׁיָּבוֹא
blocks.translit: Ani ma'amin be'emunah shleimah biviat haMashiach, ve'af al pi sheyitmahmeha, im kol zeh achakeh lo bechol yom sheyavo
blocks.ru: I believe with complete faith in the coming of Mashiach, and even though he may tarry, nevertheless I wait for him every day, that he will come

blocks.text: There is also a poetic form of the principles — the hymn **“Yigdal”** (“Exalted”), which is sung at the beginning of the morning prayer and at the end of the evening service in many communities. It is attributed to Daniel ben Yehudah of Rome (14th century). Each line of the hymn corresponds to one principle.

More on the twelfth principle can be found in the lesson “Mashiach: whom and how Judaism awaits.” In short: in Judaism Mashiach has not yet come, he is awaited, and his coming will be the first and only one; there is no “second coming” in Judaism.

“the anointed one” — a king descended from David who, according to traditional belief, will gather the exiles into the Land of Israel, rebuild the Temple and bring the world peace and the knowledge of G-d (cf. Yeshayahu 2:4; 11:1–9). Mashiach is a human being, not G-d; in Judaism he has not yet come, and he is awaited.
the resurrection of the dead at the end of days. Belief in it is expressed in the second blessing of the Amidah: “…You give life to the dead.”
Discussion and different views

The Rambam's list became the best known, but not the only one. His contemporaries and successors debated whether one can single out “main” principles at all, if the whole Torah is from G-d. Rabbi Chasdai Crescas (14th–15th centuries) built his system differently, and Rabbi Yosef Albo in the “Book of Principles” (*Sefer HaIkkarim*, 15th century) reduced the foundations to three: the existence of G-d, Torah from Heaven, and reward and punishment. Rabbi Yitzchak Abarbanel held that every commandment of the Torah is a foundation. Nevertheless, the Rambam's 13 principles are accepted in Orthodox Judaism as the generally recognized expression of traditional faith.

The movements relate to the principles differently. For Orthodoxy, all thirteen are binding foundations of faith. Conservative Judaism (the statement “Emet Ve'Emunah,” 1988) affirms belief in G-d, revelation and the covenant, but allows different understandings of *how* the Torah was given and different interpretations of Mashiach and resurrection. Reform Judaism, already in the Pittsburgh Platform of 1885, gave up belief in bodily resurrection and in a personal Mashiach, replacing them with belief in the immortality of the soul and in a coming “messianic age” of peace and justice that people bring closer through their deeds. That is why Reform siddurim often say “You give life to all” instead of “You give life to the dead.”

differs.text: Reform Judaism does not require belief in all 13 principles: instead of a personal Mashiach — a messianic age; instead of bodily resurrection — the immortality of the soul; the Torah is understood as an inspired revelation, written down by human beings.
Masorti allows different understandings of revelation (principles 8–9) and does not require a literal interpretation of principles 12–13.

blocks.text: At the beit din you may be asked to list the foundations of faith. Remember the three groups: “G-d (1–5) — Torah and prophecy (6–9) — judgment and the future (10–13).” It is even more important to explain in your own words what belief in the One G-d and in the Torah means to you.

The Rambam wrote that whoever sincerely accepts these foundations enters the community of Israel, and one must love him and treat him with brotherly compassion, even if he sins out of weakness. Faith, according to the Rambam, is not a set of words but the foundation on which an entire life according to the Torah is built.

cards.front: Where did the Rambam set out the 13 principles of faith?
cards.back: In the Commentary on the Mishnah, tractate Sanhedrin, ch. 10 (“Perek Chelek”).

cards.front: Which principles (1–5) speak about G-d?
cards.back: The existence of the Creator, unity, incorporeality, eternity, prayer to Him alone.

cards.front: Which principles (6–9) speak about the Torah and prophecy?
cards.back: Prophecy; Moshe is the greatest prophet; the Torah was given to Moshe from Heaven; the Torah is unchanging.

cards.front: Which principles (10–13) speak about judgment and the future?
cards.back: G-d's omniscience; reward and punishment; the coming of Mashiach; the resurrection of the dead.

cards.front: What does the 5th principle forbid?
cards.back: Praying to anyone other than G-d — to angels, heavenly bodies, people, intermediaries.

cards.front: What does the 7th principle affirm?
cards.back: Moshe's prophecy is the highest; there has never been, nor will there be, a prophet like him.

cards.front: How does each principle of “Ani Ma'amin” begin?
cards.back: “Ani ma'amin be'emunah shleimah” — “I believe with complete faith.”

cards.front: Which principle did prisoners of the ghettos and camps sing?
cards.back: The 12th: “Ani ma'amin… biviat haMashiach” — belief in the coming of Mashiach.

cards.front: What is “Yigdal”?
cards.back: A hymn — the poetic form of the 13 principles; attributed to Daniel ben Yehudah (Rome, 14th century).

cards.front: What does the word “Mashiach” mean?
cards.back: “The anointed one” — a king from the house of David who will gather the exiles and bring peace to the world.

cards.front: How do you say “resurrection of the dead” in Hebrew?
cards.back: Techiyat hametim (תְּחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים).

cards.front: To how many foundations did Yosef Albo reduce the faith?
cards.back: To three: the existence of G-d, Torah from Heaven, reward and punishment (“Sefer HaIkkarim”).

cards.front: How did the Pittsburgh Platform (1885) change principles 12–13?
cards.back: Instead of a personal Mashiach — a messianic age; instead of bodily resurrection — the immortality of the soul.

cards.front: Which mishnah is the Rambam commenting on when he formulates the principles?
cards.back: Sanhedrin 10:1: “All Israel have a share in the World to Come.”

cards.front: What is the name of the Conservative movement's 1988 statement of principles?
cards.back: “Emet Ve'Emunah” (“Truth and Faith”).

cards.front: According to Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1, who is denied a share in the World to Come?
cards.back: Among others — those who deny that the Torah is from Heaven.

cards.front: What does the 9th principle affirm?
cards.back: The Torah will not be replaced, and there will be no other Torah from the Creator.

cards.front: What does the 10th principle affirm?
cards.back: G-d knows all the deeds and thoughts of people (omniscience).

cards.front: When is the hymn “Yigdal” said?
cards.back: At the beginning of the morning prayer and at the end of the evening prayer in many communities.

cards.front: How does Masorti understand principles 8–9 and 12–13?
cards.back: It allows different understandings of how the Torah was given, and different interpretations of Mashiach and resurrection (“Emet Ve'Emunah,” 1988).

cards.front: What did the Rambam say about faith and life?
cards.back: Faith is not a set of words but the foundation on which an entire life according to the Torah is built.

cards.front: How does the 12th principle answer the idea of a “second coming” of Mashiach?
cards.back: Mashiach has not yet come; he is awaited every day; his coming will be the first and only one. The belief that he has already come is not Judaism.

lessons.title: G-d in Judaism: unity, the Shema, the covenant
keyIdeas: The central idea of Judaism is the One G-d; in the Ten Commandments He introduces Himself as the One who brought the people out of slavery.
The Shema (Devarim 6:4): “the L-rd is our G-d, the L-rd is One”; it is recited morning and evening as acceptance of the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven.
G-d is incorporeal; the four-letter Name is not pronounced — instead one says “Adonai” in prayer and “Hashem” in speech.
The covenants of the Torah: with Noach (the rainbow), with Avraham (brit milah), at Sinai — the Torah; the people answered “na'aseh venishma.”
Chosenness is responsibility, not superiority (Devarim 7:7–8; Amos 3:2); the goal is to emulate G-d (Sotah 14a).

blocks.text: One G-d

The central idea of Judaism is **monotheism**, faith in the one G-d. This was a revolution in the ancient world, where every people, every city and every force of nature had its own gods. The Torah teaches that the world has one Creator, Who is not part of nature but stands above it and created it. The Ten Commandments begin with the words:

blocks.he: אָנֹכִי ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם מִבֵּית עֲבָדִים
blocks.translit: Anochi Adonai Elohecha asher hotzeticha me'eretz Mitzrayim mibeit avadim
blocks.ru: I am Hashem your G-d, Who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage

blocks.text: Notice: G-d presents Himself not as “the Maker of heaven and earth,” but as the One Who *freed a people from slavery*. The G-d of the Torah is not a distant philosophical principle, but the One Who acts in history, hears the oppressed and enters into a relationship with human beings. The Rambam opens his code with the mitzvah to know that there exists a First Being Who brought all that exists into being (Mishneh Torah, Yesodei HaTorah 1:1).
Shema Yisrael
The best-known expression of Jewish faith is a verse from the book of Devarim called the **Shema**:

blocks.he: שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ ה׳ אֶחָד
blocks.translit: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad
blocks.ru: Hear, O Israel: Hashem is our G-d, Hashem is One

blocks.text: It is followed by a phrase, said in a whisper, that does not appear in the Torah but, according to tradition, was proclaimed in the Temple: “Baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed” — “Blessed is the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever.” The full recitation of the Shema consists of three passages: Devarim 6:4–9 (love of G-d, Torah study, tefillin, mezuzah), Devarim 11:13–21 (acceptance of the mitzvot, reward and punishment) and Bamidbar 15:37–41 (tzitzit and remembering the Exodus).

blocks.he: וְאָהַבְתָּ אֵת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל נַפְשְׁךָ וּבְכָל מְאֹדֶךָ
blocks.translit: Ve'ahavta et Adonai Elohecha bechol levavcha uvechol nafshecha uvechol me'odecha
blocks.ru: And you shall love Hashem your G-d with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your might

blocks.text: The Shema is recited morning and evening — “when you lie down and when you rise up” (Devarim 6:7); the entire Mishnah opens with the laws about the time for reciting it (Berachot 1:1–2). The Shema is also said before going to sleep, and it is spoken in the last moments of life. The sages call the recitation of the Shema *kabbalat ol malchut shamayim* — “accepting the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven”: every day a person acknowledges G-d anew as their King.

By tradition, men are obligated to recite the Shema at its set times; women, according to most authorities, are exempt from it as a time-bound mitzvah, but they should at least say the first verse and accept upon themselves the Kingdom of Heaven. Customs differ here.
G-d's incorporeality and His names

G-d has no body and no image. The Torah recalls Sinai: “Guard your souls very carefully, for you saw no image on the day that Hashem spoke” (Devarim 4:15). For this reason it is forbidden to depict G-d, and all expressions such as “the hand of Hashem” or “the eyes of Hashem” are, in the words of the sages, figurative language: “The Torah speaks in the language of human beings.” The Rambam explains this in detail in the Mishneh Torah (Yesodei HaTorah, ch. 1) and in the Guide for the Perplexed.

The Rambam explains the word *echad* in the Shema this way: G-d is One, but not like a species that includes many individuals, and not like a body that can be divided into parts; His oneness is unlike any other (Yesodei HaTorah 1:7). That is why, for Judaism, the doctrine of G-d in three persons is a false teaching: it falls under what the Rambam classes as *minim* — the belief that there is more than one ruler of the world (Laws of Teshuvah 3:7). The Torah says: “G-d is not a man…” (Bamidbar 23:19) — G-d does not take on a body and does not become a human being. And the words “Israel is My son, My firstborn” (Shemot 4:22) are an image of love for the whole people, not the birth of a deity. The verse “You are My son” (Tehillim 2:7) is understood the same way: it was said of King David, just as it was said of Shlomo, “I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to Me” (II Shmuel 7:14).

blocks.he: לֹא אִישׁ אֵל וִיכַזֵּב וּבֶן אָדָם וְיִתְנֶחָם
blocks.translit: Lo ish El vichazev, uven adam veyitnecham
blocks.ru: G-d is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should change His mind

blocks.text: The four-letter Name of G-d (י־ה־ו־ה) is holy, and it is not pronounced as it is written. In prayer and in the Torah reading, **Adonai** (“my L-rd”) is said in its place, and in everyday speech — **Hashem** (“the Name”). Other names: *Elohim* — G-d as Judge and Master of the forces of nature; *Shechinah* — the Divine Presence among people. Out of reverence, many people write “G-d” even in ordinary everyday writing, and texts containing holy names are not thrown away but buried (*genizah*).
The covenant — brit
covenant, alliance — mutual obligations between G-d and a person or a people.

The Torah tells of several covenants. With Noach and all of humanity — the promise never again to destroy the world by a flood; its sign is the rainbow (Bereshit 9:8–17). With Avraham — the promise that his descendants would become a people and inherit the Land of Canaan; the sign of this covenant is circumcision, *brit milah* (Bereshit 17:7–10). Finally, at Mount Sinai the whole people entered into a covenant and received the Torah. Before this G-d said:

blocks.he: וְאַתֶּם תִּהְיוּ לִי מַמְלֶכֶת כֹּהֲנִים וְגוֹי קָדוֹשׁ
blocks.translit: Ve'atem tihyu li mamlechet kohanim vegoy kadosh
blocks.ru: And you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation

blocks.text: The people answered: “All that Hashem has spoken we will do and we will hear” — *na'aseh venishma* (Shemot 24:7). The sages marvel that “we will do” came before “we will hear”: the people took on the commitment even before they knew all the details. A ger who accepts the mitzvot before the beit din repeats exactly this step.
Chosenness as responsibility

The idea of the “chosen people” is often misunderstood as superiority. The Torah itself says the opposite: “Not because you are more numerous than all the peoples did Hashem desire you… for you are the fewest of all the peoples, but because of Hashem's love for you” (Devarim 7:7–8). The prophet Amos puts it even more sharply: “You alone have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will hold you to account for all your sins” (Amos 3:2). Chosenness is not a privilege but a *task*: to live by the Torah and to be “a light to the nations” (Yeshayahu 42:6), showing the world the path of justice and holiness.

Chosenness is not racial: anyone who accepts the covenant can enter it — that is precisely why giyur exists. And the righteous of the nations of the world, according to the teaching of the sages, have a share in the World to Come even without giyur.

One of the main goals of the covenant is *imitating G-d*. The Talmud teaches: “Just as He clothes the naked, so you too clothe the naked; He visits the sick, so you too visit the sick; He comforts mourners, so you too comfort them” (Sotah 14a). A deed that glorifies G-d in people's eyes is called *kiddush Hashem* (sanctification of the Name), and one that brings Him disgrace is *chillul Hashem* (desecration of the Name).
If the beit din asks you what it means to be the “chosen people,” answer: it is responsibility and obligation, not superiority — and support this with the verses Devarim 7:7–8 and Amos 3:2.

The covenant with Israel is not “transferred” to another people, nor is it replaced by a new teaching that would cancel the Torah. The prophet Yirmiyahu, speaking of a “new covenant” (31:30–32), promises that the same Torah will be written on the heart of Israel and Yehudah. Chosenness is a responsibility, not a privilege that can be taken away from a people and given to someone else.

cards.front: The first verse of the Shema in Hebrew and in translation?
cards.back: “Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad” — “Hear, O Israel: Hashem is our G-d, Hashem is One” (Devarim 6:4).

cards.front: Which three passages make up the Shema?
cards.back: Devarim 6:4–9, Devarim 11:13–21, Bamidbar 15:37–41.

cards.front: What phrase is whispered after the first verse of the Shema?
cards.back: “Baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed.”

cards.front: When is the Shema recited?
cards.back: Morning and evening (“when you lie down and when you rise up,” Devarim 6:7), and also before going to sleep.

cards.front: What is “kabbalat ol malchut shamayim”?
cards.back: “Accepting the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven” — the sages' name for reciting the Shema.

cards.front: How does G-d present Himself in the first of the Ten Commandments?
cards.back: “I am Hashem your G-d, Who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Shemot 20:2).

cards.front: Which verse teaches that G-d has no image?
cards.back: Devarim 4:15: “you saw no image on the day that Hashem spoke.”

cards.front: What is said in place of the four-letter Name?
cards.back: In prayer — “Adonai”; in everyday speech — “Hashem.”

cards.front: What is the Shechinah?
cards.back: The Divine Presence among people.

cards.front: The sign of the covenant with Avraham?
cards.back: Brit milah — circumcision (Bereshit 17:10).

cards.front: What did the people answer at Sinai?
cards.back: “Na'aseh venishma” — “we will do and we will hear” (Shemot 24:7).

cards.front: “Mamlechet kohanim vegoy kadosh” — what is it?
cards.back: “A kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Shemot 19:6) — Israel's calling.

cards.front: How does the prophet Amos explain chosenness?
cards.back: “You alone have I known… therefore I will hold you to account for all your sins” (Amos 3:2) — chosenness as responsibility.

cards.front: What does “or lagoyim” mean?
cards.back: “A light to the nations” (Yeshayahu 42:6) — Israel's task in the world.

cards.front: What does Sotah 14a teach about imitating G-d?
cards.back: Just as G-d clothes the naked, visits the sick and comforts mourners — so should you.

cards.front: Kiddush Hashem and chillul Hashem — what are they?
cards.back: Sanctification of the Name (a deed that glorifies G-d) and desecration of the Name (one that brings Him disgrace).

cards.front: What is done with texts in which the holy Name is written?
cards.back: They are not thrown away but buried (genizah).

cards.front: What does “the Torah speaks in the language of human beings” mean?
cards.back: Expressions like “the hand of Hashem” and “the eyes of Hashem” are figurative language: G-d has no body and no image.

cards.front: What does the name Elohim signify?
cards.back: G-d as Judge and Master of the forces of nature.

cards.front: What is the essence and the sign of the covenant with Noach?
cards.back: G-d promised not to destroy the world by a flood; the sign of the covenant is the rainbow (Bereshit 9:8–17).

cards.front: Do the righteous of the nations of the world have a share in the World to Come?
cards.back: Yes, according to the teaching of the sages — even without giyur.

cards.front: What does a ger accepting the mitzvot have in common with the people at Sinai?
cards.back: The ger repeats their step — the answer “na'aseh venishma”: commitment before study.

cards.front: Is chosenness a matter of race?
cards.back: No: anyone can enter the covenant through giyur; chosenness is a task and a responsibility.

cards.front: How does the Rambam explain the word “echad” (“one”) in the Shema?
cards.back: A oneness unlike any other: not a species made up of many individuals and not a body made of parts (Yesodei HaTorah 1:7). G-d is not divided into “persons.”

cards.front: What does “Israel is My son, My firstborn” (Shemot 4:22) mean?
cards.back: An image of G-d's love for the whole people. Judaism has no literal “son of G-d,” no deity who was born.

cards.front: Of whom is “You are My son” said in Tehillim 2:7?
cards.back: Of a king from the house of David: “son” is an image of closeness, as it was said of Shlomo: “I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to Me” (II Shmuel 7:14).

cards.front: Can one say that the covenant with Israel has already been replaced and given to another people?
cards.back: No. Yirmiyahu 31 speaks of the same Torah, written on the heart of Israel. The covenant is not cancelled and not “transferred.”

lessons.title: One and indivisible: Jewish monotheism
citations: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah (Yesodei HaTorah) 1:7–1:11
Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Forbidden Relations (Issurei Bi'ah) 14:2
keyIdeas: G-d is One — not two and not more; His oneness is not like that of a species or of a body: there is nothing like Him (Rambam, Yesodei HaTorah 1:7).
G-d is incorporeal: He is not a man and does not become a man; “the hand of Hashem” is the Torah's figurative language (ibid., 1:8–1:9; Hoshea 11:9).
The Rambam's first five principles: the Creator exists, is One, is incorporeal, is the first and the last; one should pray to Him alone.
Ruach hakodesh is a level of prophetic inspiration, not a separate divine being; a human being, even Mashiach, is not G-d.
Serving anything instead of G-d or “alongside Him” is avodah zarah; it is one of the three sins one must not commit even on pain of death (Sanhedrin 74a).

blocks.text: One — and there is no other

In the lesson “G-d in Judaism: oneness, the Shema, the covenant” we spoke about the Shema: “Hashem is our G-d, Hashem is One” (Devarim (Deuteronomy) 6:4). Here we go further and ask: what does “One” mean? The Rambam answers at the very beginning of the Mishneh Torah: this G-d is One — not two and not more than two, but One. And His oneness is unlike any oneness in the world: not like a species that includes many separate individuals, and not like a body that is divided into parts and dimensions. It is a oneness that has no equal (Rambam, Yesodei HaTorah 1:7). Knowing this is a positive mitzvah in its own right, commanded by the words of the Shema (ibid., from Devarim 6:4).
“oneness” — faith in the oneness of the Almighty. Judaism professes strict monotheism: there are no “demigods” and no divine intermediaries.

blocks.he: אַתָּה הָרְאֵתָ לָדַעַת כִּי ה׳ הוּא הָאֱלֹהִים אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ
blocks.translit: Atah hor'eta lada'at ki Adonai hu ha'Elohim, ein od milvado
blocks.ru: You were shown, so that you would know that Hashem, He is G-d; there is none besides Him

blocks.text: The Torah derives G-d's oneness from what the people experienced at the Exodus: “Hashem, He is G-d; there is none besides Him” (Devarim 4:35). And more precisely still: “Hashem, He is G-d in the heavens above and on the earth below; there is no other” (Devarim 4:39). The Rambam remarks: a body cannot be above and below at the same time; since G-d is both there and there, He is not a body (ibid., 1:8).
I am the first and I am the last, and besides Me there is no G-d.

The prophets repeat the same thing. Yeshayahu (Isaiah) conveys G-d's words: “To whom, then, will you compare Me, that I should be his equal? says the Holy One” (Yeshayahu 40:25). G-d cannot be compared to anything created: any painted picture of G-d is already not G-d. “I am the first and I am the last” means that there is nothing before Him and nothing after Him. This is the fourth of the Rambam's principles, which are discussed below.
G-d is not a man

blocks.he: לֹא אִישׁ אֵל וִיכַזֵּב וּבֶן אָדָם וְיִתְנֶחָם
blocks.translit: Lo ish El vichazev, uven adam veyitnecham
blocks.ru: G-d is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should change His mind

blocks.text: The Torah says plainly that G-d is not a man: “G-d is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should change His mind” (Bamidbar (Numbers) 23:19). The prophet Hoshea (Hosea) conveys G-d's words: “for I am G-d, and not a man” (Hoshea 11:9). G-d does not take on a body and is not born. A human being — even the greatest prophet — remains a creature, not the Creator.

blocks.translit: Ki El anochi velo ish
blocks.ru: For I am G-d, and not a man

blocks.text: Hence a clear boundary. G-d is not divided into “persons,” hypostases or essences; the Rambam classes the doctrine of G-d in three persons under *minim*: this is what he calls someone who says that there are two or more rulers of the world, or that G-d has a body and an image (Laws of Teshuvah 3:7). All movements of Judaism agree on this — Orthodox, Masorti and Reform: none of them accepts a G-d in persons or a G-d-man.

The same applies to Mashiach. The future redeemer of Israel is a human being, a king from the house of David, not G-d and not a “demigod.” A separate lesson, “Mashiach: whom Judaism awaits and how,” is devoted to the topic of Mashiach; here one point is enough: no human being — including Mashiach — is G-d.

The lesson on the Shema already mentioned that at Sinai the people “saw no image” (Devarim 4:15). The Rambam gathers all the proofs together: the Torah and the prophets clearly teach that He has neither body nor form (Yesodei HaTorah 1:8).
“Hand,” “eyes,” “under His feet”

blocks.translit: Dibrah Torah kilshon bnei adam
blocks.ru: The Torah speaks in the language of human beings

blocks.text: What should we make of the places in the Torah that speak of “the hand of Hashem,” “the eyes of Hashem,” “under His feet”? The Rambam answers: the Torah speaks in the language of human beings (Yesodei HaTorah 1:9). The words are human, so that a person can understand; the meaning is beyond any image. The visions of the prophets are “prophetic vision and parable,” not a photograph of Heaven.

More follows from incorporeality than it might seem. Since He has no body, bodily events do not apply to Him: there is no joining and separating, no place and measure, no ascending and descending, no right and left side, no beginning and end. And He does not change: “For I, Hashem, have not changed” (Malachi 3:6; Rambam, Yesodei HaTorah 1:11).

blocks.translit: Ki ani Adonai lo shaniti
blocks.ru: For I, Hashem, have not changed

blocks.text: The first five principles
The Rambam's 13 Principles of Faith (see the lesson devoted to them) begin with five statements about G-d:

items: The Creator exists, and He is the cause of all that exists.
He is One — with a oneness that has no equal.
He has no body and no likeness of a body.
He is the first and the last.
One should pray to Him alone, and not to any other being.

blocks.he: שֶׁהַבּוֹרֵא יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ אֵינוֹ גוּף, וְלֹא יַשִּׂיגוּהוּ מַשִּׂיגֵי הַגּוּף, וְאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם דִּמְיוֹן כְּלָל
blocks.translit: She'haBorei yitbarach shemo eino guf, velo yasiguhu masigei haguf, ve'ein lo shum dimyon klal
blocks.ru: That the Creator, blessed be His Name, is not a body, that the properties of a body do not apply to Him, and that He has no likeness whatsoever

blocks.text: “the spirit of holiness” — a level of prophetic inspiration that the Creator grants a person; not a separate divine being and not a “person.”

In the siddur the third principle reads: the Creator “is not a body, and He has no likeness whatsoever.” The concept of ruach hakodesh sometimes confuses people coming from other traditions: in Judaism it is a level of prophetic inspiration that the Creator grants a person — not a separate divine being and not a “person.” And the fifth principle explicitly forbids addressing prayer to anyone “between” a person and G-d: one should pray to Him alone.
Avodah zarah — a line that must never be crossed
“foreign worship” — worshipping anything instead of G-d: a human being, an image, any created thing, or an “intermediary” alongside Him.

blocks.he: לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים עַל פָּנָי
blocks.translit: Lo yihyeh lecha elohim acherim al panai
blocks.ru: You shall have no other gods before My presence

blocks.text: The Ten Commandments open with a prohibition: “You shall have no other gods before My presence” (Shemot (Exodus) 20:3–5). Serving anything instead of G-d — or “together with Him,” “alongside Him” — is called avodah zarah, “foreign worship.” The Talmud counts avodah zarah among the three sins that a Jew must not commit even on pain of death — together with murder and forbidden relations (Sanhedrin 74a).

Therefore teachings that alter the very oneness of G-d — about G-d in three persons, about G-d who became a man, about a divine messiah, about praying through intermediaries — are not Judaism, even if Jewish words and verses of the Tanakh are heard in them (Rambam, Laws of Teshuvah 3:7). A candidate for giyur is given a detailed explanation of G-d's oneness and of the prohibition of avodah zarah (Rambam, Laws of Forbidden Relations 14:2).
“partnership” — associating another being with the worship of the Creator.

Shituf means “partnership,” that is, associating another being with the worship of the Creator. For a Jew — and therefore also for a ger after giyur — any shituf is forbidden. Whether shituf should be considered forbidden for non-Jews is debated by the authorities: Tosafot (Sanhedrin 63b) and the Rema (Orach Chaim 156:1) lean towards leniency, while many understand the Rambam more strictly.
Verses that are often reinterpreted

Anyone who studies Judaism will sooner or later hear the claim that the Tanakh itself hints at “plurality” in G-d. It is useful to know how the Jewish tradition answers this, reading the verses in their own context.

items: **“Elohim” is a plural form.** It is a form expressing majesty and fullness of power; when it refers to the Almighty, the verb is in the singular: “In the beginning G-d created (*bara*)” (Bereshit 1:1). The Torah uses the same word for a single human being: “I have made you *elohim* to Pharaoh” (Shemot 7:1).

**“Let us make man” (Bereshit 1:26).** Rashi explains: the Almighty “consulted” His retinue — the angels — in order to teach people humility. And the very next verse speaks in the singular: “And G-d created man” (Bereshit 1:27).
**Avraham's three guests (Bereshit 18).** They are angel-messengers, each with his own mission (Rashi on Bereshit 18:2); further on the Torah explicitly calls them angels (Bereshit 19:1).

**“Echad” as a “compound unity.”** Sometimes it is compared with the words “and they shall become one flesh” (Bereshit 2:24). But the Rambam explains G-d's oneness precisely as one that is not made up of parts and is unlike any other (Yesodei HaTorah 1:7), and the Torah adds: “there is none besides Him” (Devarim 4:35).

blocks.text: Miracles and beautiful interpretations do not prove a teaching. The Torah warns: if a prophet appears and gives a sign, and it comes true, but he calls you to serve other gods — “do not listen to the words of that prophet, for Hashem is testing you” (Devarim 13:2–4). The Rambam extends this to a prophet who declares that the mitzvot of the Torah have been abolished or changed (Yesodei HaTorah 9:1–3). The Rambam writes that Israel's faith in Moshe rests not on miracles, but on the fact that the whole people heard Sinai for themselves (Yesodei HaTorah 8:1).

At the beit din you may be asked: “What do you believe about G-d?” Or, if you grew up in another faith: “How do you now relate to your former faith?” Answer calmly and clearly: “I believe in one G-d, indivisible, without body or form; I pray only to Him; I do not accept the teaching of G-d in three persons or the idea that G-d became a man; I respect my family, but I no longer take part in other religious services.”

cards.front: How does the Rambam formulate the unity of G-d (Yesodei HaTorah 1:7)?
cards.back: G-d is One — not two and not more than two; His unity is not like that of a species or of a body: there is nothing like Him in the world.

cards.front: Which mitzvah is connected with knowing the unity of G-d?
cards.back: The positive mitzvah to know that G-d is One; it is derived from the words of the Shema (Devarim 6:4; Rambam, Yesodei HaTorah 1:7).

cards.front: Complete the verse: “The L-rd, He is G-d, …”
cards.back: “…there is none besides Him” (Devarim 4:35).

cards.front: How does the Rambam (Yesodei HaTorah 1:8) prove G-d's incorporeality from Devarim 4:39?
cards.back: G-d is “in the heavens above and on the earth below”; a body cannot be in two places at once, so He is not a body.

cards.front: What does “I am the first and I am the last” (Yeshayahu 44:6) mean?
cards.back: There is nothing before Him and nothing after Him; besides Him there is no G-d. This is the Rambam's fourth principle.

cards.front: What does “the Torah speaks in human language” (Yesodei HaTorah 1:9) mean?
cards.back: “The hand of the L-rd”, “the eyes of the L-rd” are figurative human language; G-d has no body, and the visions of the prophets are parables.

cards.front: According to the Rambam (Yesodei HaTorah 1:11), what cannot be applied to G-d?
cards.back: Joining and separation, place and measure, ascent and descent, right and left, beginning and end; He does not change (Malachi 3:6).

cards.front: Where does the Torah say: “G-d is not a man, that He should lie”?
cards.back: Bamidbar 23:19: G-d is not a man nor a son of man — He does not lie and does not change His mind.

cards.front: What is the essence of the third of the Rambam's 13 principles?
cards.back: The Creator is not a body and has no likeness whatsoever (the “Ani Maamin” formula in the siddur).

cards.front: What is the essence of the fifth of the Rambam's 13 principles?
cards.back: One should pray only to G-d and not to any other being; intermediaries are not permitted.

cards.front: What is ruach hakodesh?
cards.back: “The spirit of holiness” — a level of prophetic inspiration that the Creator grants a person; not a separate divine being.

cards.front: What is avodah zarah?
cards.back: “Foreign worship” — worshipping a human being, an image or a created thing as G-d, or as an intermediary between a person and G-d.

cards.front: What are the three sins one must not commit even on pain of death?
cards.back: Avodah zarah, murder and forbidden relations (Sanhedrin 74a).

cards.front: Who is Mashiach according to the teaching of Judaism?
cards.back: A human being — a king from the House of David, not G-d (see the lesson “Mashiach: whom Judaism awaits and how”).

cards.front: How do all the movements of Judaism relate to monotheism?
cards.back: All the movements — Orthodox, Masorti and Reform — profess strict monotheism; none of them accepts G-d in three persons or a G-d-man.

cards.front: What is shituf, and what is its status for a Jew and for a ger?
cards.back: “Partnership” — associating another being with the worship of the Creator. For a Jew, and for a ger after giyur, any shituf is forbidden.

cards.front: Why does the plural form “Elohim” not mean “many gods”?
cards.back: It is a form of majesty; the verb used with the Almighty is singular: “bara Elohim” (Bereshit 1:1).

cards.front: How does Rashi explain “Let us make man” (Bereshit 1:26)?
cards.back: The Almighty “consulted” with the angels to teach humility; the next verse is in the singular: “and He created”.

cards.front: Does a miracle prove a prophet right if he abolishes mitzvot of the Torah?
cards.back: No: “do not listen to the words of that prophet, for the L-rd your G-d is testing you” (Devarim 13:2–4). Faith rests on Sinai (Rambam, Yesodei HaTorah 8:1).

lessons.title: Mashiach: whom Judaism awaits and how
citations: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings and Their Wars 11:1
Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 11:3–4
Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 12:1–2, 12:4–5
Rambam, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin, ch. 10, principles 12–13
Siddur, “Ani Maamin”, principle 12; Amidah, the blessing “Et Tzemach David”
keyIdeas: Judaism awaits Mashiach — and awaits him for the first time: he has not yet come. There is no concept of a “second coming” in Judaism.
Mashiach is a human being, a king from the House of David, not a deity and not an intermediary; he will die, and his son and grandson will reign after him (Rambam).
The Rambam's criteria: restore the kingdom of David, build the Temple, gather the exiles; Judaism judges Mashiach by results in this world.
To wait means to hope every day (“Ani Maamin”, the Amidah) and to live by the Torah already now; one does not calculate the time of his coming (Sanhedrin 97b).
The movements understand Mashiach differently (a person or a messianic era), but they are united on the main point: Mashiach has not yet come.

blocks.text: Whom does Judaism await?

The word **mashiach** (מָשִׁיחַ) means “anointed one”: kings and the High Priest were anointed with consecrated oil, and the anointing dedicated a person to service. Mashiach is the future anointed king whom Israel awaits. The anticipation of him is voiced in daily prayer and in the twelfth of the Rambam's thirteen principles of faith. And the main point must be stated right away and clearly: **Mashiach has not yet come.** His coming lies in the future, and it will be the first and only one.

Mashiach is a human being: he will be born and will die, like every person. He is not a deity and not an intermediary to whom one addresses prayer: the Rambam's fifth principle teaches that one may pray only to the Almighty. The Rambam writes in his introduction to the chapter of Sanhedrin devoted to the principles of faith: Mashiach will die, and his son and grandson will reign after him (Rambam, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin, ch. 10).

“anointed one” — the future king descended from David, who will gather the exiles into the Land of Israel, restore the Temple, and bring the world peace and the knowledge of G-d. In Judaism Mashiach has not yet come; he is awaited.
What the prophets say

The prophets paint the image of the future king. Yeshayahu (Isaiah) speaks of him as a shoot from the stump of Yishai (Jesse), David's father: the kingdom of David will be like a felled tree, from whose stump a new sprout will grow.

blocks.he: וְיָצָא חֹטֶר מִגֵּזַע יִשָׁי וְנֵצֶר מִשָּׁרָשָׁיו יִפְרֶה. וְנָחָה עָלָיו רוּחַ ה׳
blocks.translit: Veyatza choter migeza Yishai, venetzer misharashav yifreh; venachah alav ruach Adonai
blocks.ru: And a shoot shall come forth from the stump of Yishai, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit; and the spirit of the L-rd shall rest upon him

blocks.text: The prophets speak of the time of Mashiach as a time of peace and of the knowledge of G-d. Mashiach will gather the dispersed of Israel “from the four corners of the earth” (Yeshayahu 11:12); the nations “shall beat their swords into plowshares” — “nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more” (Yeshayahu 2:4). Yirmiyahu (Jeremiah) calls him “a righteous shoot of David” (Yirmiyahu 23:5–6), and Yechezkel (Ezekiel) promises: “My servant David shall be king over them” forever, and G-d's sanctuary shall be in their midst (Yechezkel 37:24–28).
For the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the L-rd, as the waters cover the sea.
How it will be: the words of the Rambam

The fullest description was given by the Rambam in the “Mishneh Torah”, in the Laws of Kings: “King Mashiach will arise and restore the kingdom of David to its former glory, build the Temple and gather all the exiles of Israel.” All the mitzvot of the Torah will once again be observed as before (Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:1). The same Rambam stresses: whoever does not believe in Mashiach or does not await his coming denies not only the words of the prophets, but the Torah itself and Moshe (ibid., 11:1).

At the same time, there is no need to expect miracles. “Do not think that King Mashiach must perform signs and wonders or revive the dead,” the Rambam warns. Rabbi Akiva, the great sage of the Mishnah, and all the sages of his generation considered Bar Kochba to be King Mashiach and demanded of him neither sign nor wonder; when Bar Kochba was killed, it became clear that it was not he (Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:3).
How can Mashiach be recognized? The Rambam lists the criteria (Laws of Kings 11:4):

items: A king arises from the House of David: he occupies himself with Torah and observes the mitzvot like his ancestor David, according to the Written and the Oral Torah;
he will lead all of Israel to walk in its way and repairs its breaches;
he fights the wars of G-d. Then he is “presumed to be Mashiach” (bechezkat mashiach).
If he has done all this and succeeded, built the Temple on its site and gathered the exiles of Israel, he is certainly Mashiach.
But if he did not succeed to that extent or was killed, it is clear that he is not the one the Torah promised.

blocks.text: The logic here is strict: Judaism judges by results in this world. The Temple has not been restored, the exiles have not been gathered, so Mashiach has not yet come. And one who began but did not complete these tasks, or was killed, was not Mashiach according to the Rambam (Laws of Kings 11:4). This makes clear why belief in a Mashiach who supposedly already came, died and will return “a second time” contradicts the very definition of Mashiach and the twelfth principle; for Judaism this is a false teaching. Mashiach will come once, and it will be his first and only coming.

“presumed to be Mashiach” — the status of a king from the House of David who meets the Rambam's criteria but has not yet completed the tasks of Mashiach: the Temple has not been built, the exiles have not been gathered (Laws of Kings 11:4).
What will change in the days of Mashiach?

The prophets' words about the world are sometimes taken literally. The Rambam is cautious: “the order of the world will not change” — in Hebrew עוֹלָם כְּמִנְהָגוֹ נוֹהֵג, “the world will follow its usual course” (Laws of Kings 12:1). The famous “the wolf shall dwell with the lamb” (Yeshayahu 11:6), he explains, is a parable: Israel will live securely among the nations that were once like wolves toward it.

blocks.translit: Olam keminhago noheg
blocks.ru: The world will follow its usual order

blocks.text: The Talmud conveys almost the same thing: there is no difference between this world and the days of Mashiach except one — the end of subjugation to foreign kingdoms (the view of Shmuel, Talmud, Berachot 34b; the Rambam adopts it in the Laws of Kings 12:2). Before Mashiach, the prophet Eliyahu will come as forerunner and herald. The Rambam adds: no one knows how all this will be until it happens (Laws of Kings 12:2).

So what is all this for? Not for power and not for pleasures: “the sages and prophets did not long for the days of Mashiach in order to rule over the world, or to eat and drink, but in order to be free for the Torah and its wisdom” (ibid., 12:4). In those days there will be neither famine nor war, neither envy nor rivalry; the sole occupation of the world will be to know the Almighty — “for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the L-rd” (Yeshayahu 11:9; Rambam, ibid., 12:5).

There is also a more miraculous picture: the aggadah says that if Israel is worthy, Mashiach will come “with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13), and if not, poor and riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9) (Talmud, Sanhedrin 98a). The resurrection of the dead — techiyat hametim — is the thirteenth principle of faith, a separate event expected later; Mashiach does not have to revive the dead in order to be recognized (Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:3; Commentary on the Mishnah, principle 13).

the resurrection of the dead at the end of days, the thirteenth principle of faith. A separate event, expected after the coming of Mashiach; Mashiach does not have to revive the dead in order to be recognized (Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:3).
How to wait?
Awaiting Mashiach is a daily matter, not an abstract dogma. The twelfth principle of faith reads:

blocks.he: אֲנִי מַאֲמִין בֶּאֱמוּנָה שְׁלֵמָה בְּבִיאַת הַמָּשִׁיחַ, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיִּתְמַהְמֵהַּ, עִם כָּל זֶה אֲחַכֶּה לּוֹ בְּכָל יוֹם שֶׁיָּבוֹא
blocks.translit: Ani ma'amin be'emunah shleimah biviat haMashiach, ve'af al pi sheyitmahmeha, im kol zeh achakeh lo bechol yom sheyavo
blocks.ru: I believe with complete faith in the coming of Mashiach, and even though he may tarry, nevertheless I wait for him every day, that he will come

blocks.text: “Though he may tarry” — the wait is long, lasting centuries, and still “I wait for him every day.” Three times a day, in the standing prayer, the Amidah, there is the blessing “Et Tzemach David”: “Cause the offspring of David, Your servant, to flourish speedily, and exalt his horn through Your salvation, for we hope for Your salvation all day long” (Siddur, Amidah). Beside it stand the blessings for the ingathering of the exiles and for the rebuilding of Jerusalem: “and speedily establish the throne of David within it.”

blocks.translit: Ki lishuatcha kivinu kol hayom
blocks.ru: For we hope for Your salvation all day long
blocks.ref: Siddur, Amidah, the blessing “Et Tzemach David”

blocks.text: Did you hope for redemption? (צִפִּיתָ לִישׁוּעָה?)

The hope for redemption is so essential that a person is asked about it at the Heavenly Court: tractate Shabbat says that among the questions put to a person are whether they conducted their business honestly, whether they set aside time for Torah, and whether they hoped for redemption (Talmud, Shabbat 31a). Waiting does not mean sitting with folded hands: while awaiting Mashiach, a person learns Torah, observes the mitzvot and makes the world around them kinder. That is both the meaning of the hope and the work itself.
When?
May the bones of those who calculate the end be blasted. (תִּיפַּח עַצְמָן שֶׁל מְחַשְּׁבֵי קִצִּין)

Calculating dates is not merely futile but condemned: no one knows how all this will be until it happens (Rambam, Laws of Kings 12:2). One episode in the Talmud says it better than any argument. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi met Mashiach and asked: “When will the master come?” The answer was: “Today.” When that day passed, the prophet Eliyahu explained Mashiach's words to the rabbi with a verse from Tehillim: “today, if you will listen to His voice” (Tehillim 95:7; Talmud, Sanhedrin 98a). “Today” depends on us — on how we live.

In the same place the Talmud interprets the words of Yeshayahu: “in its time I will hasten it” (Yeshayahu 60:22). If Israel is worthy, “I will hasten it”; if not, he will come “in its time” (Talmud, Sanhedrin 98a). Only the Almighty knows the time.
What history teaches

History knows of hopes that did not stand the test of the criteria. Bar Kochba, the hero of the 2nd-century revolt, whom Rabbi Akiva considered Mashiach, was killed in the war, and the hope faded (Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:3). In 1665–1666 thousands of Jews believed in Shabtai Tzvi, who proclaimed himself Mashiach; soon afterward he converted to Islam. For Judaism this is not a mystery but a confirmation of the rule: Mashiach is recognized by completed deeds, not by the excitement of a crowd. And the Temple still does not stand.
Verses that are often reinterpreted
Candidates for giyur are often told that the prophets “already described” a Mashiach who came, suffered and will return. The Jewish answer is to read the verses themselves in their context:

items: **“Behold, the young woman shall conceive” (Yeshayahu 7:14).** In Hebrew, *almah* means “young woman”, not a special word for a virgin. It is a sign to King Achaz in his own time: “before the boy knows to refuse evil… the land shall be deserted” of the two hostile kings (Yeshayahu 7:16).

**The suffering “servant of the L-rd” (Yeshayahu 52:13–53:12).** Yeshayahu himself calls the people the “servant”: “You are My servant, Israel” (Yeshayahu 49:3; 41:8). This is also how Rashi explains the chapter: it speaks of the people of Israel, who suffered among the nations.

**Forgiveness through faith in another's death.** The Torah teaches that each person is responsible for themselves: “The soul that sins, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Yechezkel 18:20; Devarim 24:16). The path of atonement is teshuvah, returning to the Almighty, and prayer: “instead of bulls, the words of our lips” (Hoshea 14:3).
