**Tehillim 22:17.** The Hebrew text reads *ka'ari*, “like a lion (they maul) my hands and my feet”, not “they pierced”. This is David's lament, which ends with praise in the congregation of Israel.
**Tehillim 110:1.** “The L-rd said to my lord” — in Hebrew *la'adoni*, “to my master”, a human form of address, not the Name *Adonai*. Rashi relates the psalm to Avraham.
**Daniel 9:24–27.** Rashi reads the “seventy weeks” as a period surrounding the First and Second Temples, not as proof that Mashiach has already come.
**Yirmiyahu 31:30–32.** The “new covenant” is the same Torah written on the heart of Israel, not the abolition of the mitzvot and not the transfer of the covenant to another people.
**Michah 5:1.** The ruler from Beit Lechem is a human leader from the line of David; “whose origins are from of old” speaks of the antiquity of the lineage, not of a deity.
**Zechariah 12:10.** The commentators relate the mourning “as for an only son” to the fallen or to a human redeemer who will die in battle, not to G-d having been “pierced”.

blocks.text: Sometimes preachers put on a tallit, blow the shofar and celebrate Pesach, while teaching that Mashiach has already come. Jewish words and rituals do not change the substance: belief in a Mashiach who has already come contradicts the twelfth principle and is not Judaism (Rambam, 13 Principles, the 12th).
How the movements see it

Orthodox Judaism understands all of this literally, as binding belief: the twelfth principle is part of the foundations. The Conservative movement, in its statement “Emet Ve-Emunah” (1988), speaks of the hope for messianic redemption and allows for different understandings of a personal Mashiach. Reform Judaism, in the Pittsburgh Platform (1885), replaced the expectation of a personal Mashiach with the hope for a messianic era of peace and justice, brought nearer by human deeds.

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, instead of a personal Mashiach, people await a messianic era of peace and justice, brought nearer by human actions (Pittsburgh Platform, 1885).
In Conservative Judaism (Masorti) there is a hope for messianic redemption, while the understanding of a personal Mashiach is left to the individual believer (“Emet Ve-Emunah”, 1988).

blocks.text: But in all the movements the main point is the same: Mashiach has not yet come, and no person in the past was Mashiach. That is why there is no concept of a “second coming” in Judaism: one who has never come cannot come “a second time”. Many people confuse these things; it is important for a candidate for giyur to understand the difference clearly and calmly.

At the beit din you may be asked whether Mashiach has come and what Judaism awaits. Answer calmly and in your own words: “Mashiach has not yet come. I await his coming, and it will be the first and only one. Mashiach is a human being, a king from the House of David, not a deity and not an intermediary. I do not share the belief in a Mashiach who supposedly already came and will return: that is not Judaism.” Keep your respect for relatives of another faith; there is no need for polemics at the beit din.

cards.front: What does the word “mashiach” (מָשִׁיחַ) mean?
cards.back: “Anointed one”: kings and the High Priest were anointed with oil; Mashiach is the future anointed king.

cards.front: Who is Mashiach according to Jewish belief?
cards.back: A human being, a king descended from David; not a deity and not an intermediary to whom one prays (Rambam, Sanhedrin, ch. 10).

cards.front: Has Mashiach come?
cards.back: No. The Temple has not been restored, the exiles have not been gathered — the Rambam's criteria (11:4) have not been met.

cards.front: How many comings of Mashiach does Judaism await?
cards.back: One, and it is still ahead. There is no concept of a “second coming” in Judaism.

cards.front: What does the Rambam say about the death of Mashiach?
cards.back: Mashiach will die, and his son and grandson will reign after him (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin, ch. 10).

cards.front: What must Mashiach do according to the Rambam (11:1)?
cards.back: Restore the kingdom of David, build the Temple, gather the exiles of Israel; the Torah will be observed as before.

cards.front: What does the status “bechezkat mashiach” (11:4) mean?
cards.back: “Presumed to be Mashiach”: a king from the House of David teaches Torah, strengthens it and fights the wars of G-d, but has not yet proven himself conclusively.

cards.front: Must Mashiach perform miracles and revive the dead?
cards.back: No (Rambam 11:3). Rabbi Akiva believed in Bar Kochba, but he fell, and the hope was not fulfilled.

cards.front: What will NOT change in the days of Mashiach?
cards.back: The order of the world: “olam keminhago noheg” (12:1); according to Berachot 34b, only subjugation to foreign kingdoms will end.

cards.front: What two pictures of Mashiach's coming are found in the aggadah?
cards.back: If Israel is worthy, “with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13); if not, poor and riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9). Sanhedrin 98a.

cards.front: How does the 12th principle of “Ani Maamin” read?
cards.back: “Though he may tarry, I wait for him every day, that he will come” — to await Mashiach every day.

cards.front: Which blessing of the Amidah is connected with Mashiach?
cards.back: “Et Tzemach David”: “for we hope for Your salvation all day long” (כִּי לִישׁוּעָתְךָ קִוִּינוּ כָּל הַיּוֹם).

cards.front: What question about Mashiach is asked at the Heavenly Court?
cards.back: “Did you hope for redemption?” (צִפִּיתָ לִישׁוּעָה) — Talmud, Shabbat 31a.

cards.front: What does it mean to await Mashiach?
cards.back: Not to wait with folded hands, but to live by the Torah already now and to hope every day.

cards.front: What is said about calculating the time of Mashiach's coming?
cards.back: “May the bones of those who calculate the end rot away” (Sanhedrin 97b); Rambam 12:2: do not calculate the end.

cards.front: How did Eliyahu explain Mashiach’s answer, “Today”?
cards.back: “Today, if you will listen to His voice” (Tehillim 95:7; Sanhedrin 98a): “today” depends on us.

cards.front: How do the different movements understand Mashiach?
cards.back: Orthodoxy: belief in a personal Mashiach is obligatory; Masorti (“Emet ve-Emunah,” 1988): a range of understandings; Reform (1885): a messianic age that people bring closer. Common to all: he has not yet come.

cards.front: How should you answer at the beit din if asked whether Mashiach has come?
cards.back: Calmly: he has not yet come; I await his coming; he will be the first and only one; Mashiach is a human being, a king from the house of David.

cards.front: What does the word *almah* mean in Yeshayahu 7:14?
cards.back: “A young woman.” It is a sign to King Ahaz in his own time (Yeshayahu 7:16), not a prediction about the distant future.

cards.front: According to Jewish interpretation, who is the “servant of Hashem” in Yeshayahu 53?
cards.back: The people of Israel: “You are My servant, Israel” (Yeshayahu 49:3); Rashi explains it this way as well.

cards.front: Is belief in the atoning death of another person needed for the forgiveness of sins?
cards.back: No: each person answers for himself (Yechezkel 18:20), and the path to forgiveness is teshuvah and prayer (Hoshea 14:3).

cards.front: Do Jewish rituals turn the teaching of a Mashiach who has “already come” into Judaism?
cards.back: No. A tallit and a shofar do not change the essence: belief in a Mashiach who has already come contradicts the 12th principle.

cards.front: What does the Hebrew say in Tehillim 22:17: *ka’ari* or “they pierced”?
cards.back: *Ka’ari*, “like a lion.” This is David’s lament, not a description of an execution.

cards.front: Whom does *adoni* refer to in Tehillim 110:1?
cards.back: A human “lord,” not the Divine Name. The psalm does not introduce a second “person” of G-d.

lessons.title: A Brief History of the Jewish People
keyIdeas: Whoever joins the people also takes on its history: in the Pesach Haggadah, every person must see himself as if he himself had come out of Egypt.
From Avraham (“lech lecha”) to the twelve tribes of Yaakov-Israel; the Exodus is remembered on Pesach, the giving of the Torah on Shavuot.
Shlomo built the First Temple; it was destroyed in 586 BCE, and the Second in 70 CE; in Yavneh the Torah was preserved, and prayer took the place of sacrifices.
Almost two thousand years of diaspora: Ashkenazim and Sephardim, persecution, Chasidim and Mitnagdim, emancipation and new movements.
The Shoah: the murder of about six million Jews; in 1948 the State of Israel was proclaimed; a ger becomes part of this history.

blocks.text: One who joins the Jewish people takes on not only its faith and commandments but also its *history*: the Pesach Haggadah says that every person must see himself as if he himself had come out of Egypt. Below are the main milestones of this history. Dates for the ancient period follow the generally accepted scholarly chronology; the traditional Jewish count of years (from the creation of the world) sometimes differs for early events.
The Patriarchs and Matriarchs

The history of the people begins with **Avraham**, a man from Mesopotamia (Ur Kasdim, then Haran) who, according to tradition, came to faith in the One G-d on his own and smashed his father’s idols. G-d said to him:

blocks.he: לֶךְ לְךָ מֵאַרְצְךָ וּמִמּוֹלַדְתְּךָ וּמִבֵּית אָבִיךָ אֶל הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ
blocks.translit: Lech lecha me’artzecha u’mimoladtecha u’mibeit avicha el ha’aretz asher ar’eka
blocks.ru: Go from your land, from your birthplace and from your father’s house, to the land that I will show you

blocks.text: The patriarchs are **Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov**; the matriarchs are **Sarah, Rivka, Rachel and Leah**. Yaakov received the name **Israel** (Bereshit 32:29), and his twelve sons became the founders of the twelve tribes of Israel. The name “Hebrews” (*ivrim*) is traditionally linked to the word *ever*, “the other side”: Avraham “stood on one side, and the whole world on the other.” From the tribe of Yehudah (Judah) comes the word “Jew,” *Yehudi*.
Egypt, the Exodus and Sinai

During a famine Yaakov and his family moved to Egypt, where in time his descendants became slaves. Through **Moshe** (Moses) and his brother **Aharon**, G-d brought the people out of slavery, after the ten plagues of Egypt and the splitting of the Red Sea (the Sea of Reeds) (Shemot 12–14). This event is remembered on Pesach, and the memory of the Exodus resounds in the kiddush, in the Shema and in many mitzvot. Seven weeks after the Exodus, at Mount **Sinai**, the people received the Torah and heard the Ten Commandments (Shemot 19–20); this is celebrated on Shavuot. The forty years of wandering in the wilderness are remembered on Sukkot.
The Land of Israel and the First Temple

Under the leadership of **Yehoshua bin Nun** the people entered Canaan. Then came the period of the Judges, and around the 11th–10th centuries BCE a kingdom arose: the first king was Shaul (Saul), then **David**, who made **Jerusalem** his capital, and his son **Shlomo** (Solomon), who built the **First Temple** (Melachim I 6). After Shlomo’s death the kingdom split into the Kingdom of Israel (northern, ten tribes) and the Kingdom of Judah (southern). In 722 BCE Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom, and its inhabitants were scattered. In 586 BCE the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem and the First Temple and carried the Judeans off into the **Babylonian exile** (Melachim II 25).

blocks.translit: Im eshkachech Yerushalayim, tishkach yemini
blocks.ru: If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill

blocks.text: The Second Temple and Its Destruction

In 538 BCE the Persian king Cyrus allowed the Jews to return (Ezra 1:1–4); the Second Temple was dedicated around 516 BCE. Ezra and Nechemiah restored life according to the Torah. In the 2nd century BCE the Hasmoneans (Maccabees) rose up against the Greco-Syrian king Antiochus IV, who had banned Judaism, and in 164 BCE they purified the Temple; this is the origin of Chanukah. Later Judea came under the rule of Rome. In 70 CE the Romans under the command of Titus destroyed the Second Temple. According to tradition, both Temples were destroyed on the 9th of Av, the saddest day of the Jewish calendar.

Judaism survived this catastrophe thanks to the sages. Shortly before the fall of Jerusalem, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asked the Romans for the town of **Yavneh** and its sages (Gittin 56b), and there the tradition of the Torah was preserved. Prayer replaced the sacrifices, and the synagogue and the house of study became the center of life. The Bar Kochba revolt (132–135) was brutally crushed, Rabbi Akiva died a martyr’s death, and Jews were forbidden to enter Jerusalem.
Exile and Diaspora

For almost two thousand years most Jews lived in the **diaspora** (*galut*, “exile”). The great centers were Babylonia (where the Babylonian Talmud was composed), and then Muslim Spain, with its “golden age” of poetry and philosophy (Yehudah HaLevi, Ibn Ezra, Rambam). Two main cultural branches took shape: the **Ashkenazim** (Germany, France, later Poland, Lithuania, Russia) and the **Sephardim** (Spain, Portugal, and after the expulsion of 1492, the Ottoman Empire, North Africa, the Netherlands), as well as the Eastern communities (*Mizrachim*). The Middle Ages and the modern era brought both flourishing and persecution: the Crusades, blood libels, expulsions from England, France and Spain, and the Chmielnicki massacres (1648–1649).

In the 18th century **Chasidism** arose in Eastern Europe (its founder was Israel Baal Shem Tov, c. 1698–1760), while its opponents, the *Mitnagdim*, led by the Vilna Gaon (1720–1797), developed the scholarship of the Lithuanian yeshivot. In the Russian Empire, Jews lived in the Pale of Settlement (from the end of the 18th century) and suffered pogroms and restrictions; many emigrated to America. Emancipation in Western Europe gave Jews civil rights and gave rise to new movements in Judaism. In the Soviet Union religion was persecuted, but Jewish identity survived, and in the 1970s–1990s hundreds of thousands of Jews made aliyah to Israel.
The Shoah

In 1933–1945 Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about **six million Jews**, a third of the Jewish people. This is called the **Shoah** (the Catastrophe) or the Holocaust. Entire communities of Europe were wiped out, including in the occupied territories of the USSR (Babi Yar, the ghettos of Minsk, Vilnius and many other cities). The Day of Remembrance of the Holocaust and Heroism, *Yom HaShoah*, is observed on 27 Nisan; International Holocaust Remembrance Day is January 27, the day Auschwitz was liberated.
The State of Israel

The dream of returning to Zion resounded in every prayer. At the end of the 19th century political **Zionism** emerged; Theodor Herzl convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel (1897). On **May 14, 1948** (5 Iyar 5708), David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the establishment of the **State of Israel**: the return of the people to sovereignty in its own Land. This day is celebrated as Yom HaAtzmaut, a day of thanksgiving. In 1967, in the Six-Day War, Israel reunited Jerusalem, the eternal and undivided capital of the Jewish people, and Jews could once again pray at the Western Wall (the Kotel), a remnant of the wall surrounding the Temple Mount. The Law of Return (1950) grants the right to immigrate to Israel to every Jew, including those who have undergone giyur.

A ger becomes part of this entire history. As Ruth said: “Your people is my people.” At the beit din you may be asked whether you understand that you are joining a people that has suffered greatly, has returned to its Land and still defends it, and that love for Eretz Israel is part of this path.

cards.front: Name the patriarchs and matriarchs.
cards.back: Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov; Sarah, Rivka, Rachel, Leah.

cards.front: What second name did Yaakov receive?
cards.back: Israel (Bereshit 32:29).

cards.front: With what words did G-d address Avraham?
cards.back: “Lech lecha”: “Go from your land…” (Bereshit 12:1).

cards.front: Which festival is connected with the Exodus, and which with Sinai?
cards.back: The Exodus: Pesach; the giving of the Torah: Shavuot.

cards.front: Who built the First Temple?
cards.back: King Shlomo (Solomon), the son of David.

cards.front: Who destroyed the First Temple, and when?
cards.back: The Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar, 586 BCE.

cards.front: Who allowed the Jews to return from Babylonia?
cards.back: The Persian king Cyrus, 538 BCE (Ezra 1).

cards.back: The Hasmonean revolt against Antiochus IV and the purification of the Temple (164 BCE).

cards.front: When was the Second Temple destroyed?
cards.back: In 70 CE, by the Romans (Titus); according to tradition, on the 9th of Av, like the First.

cards.front: What did Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai do?
cards.back: He asked the Romans for Yavneh and its sages and preserved the tradition of the Torah after the destruction of the Temple.

cards.front: Ashkenazim and Sephardim: who are they?
cards.back: Ashkenazim are the Jews of Central and Eastern Europe; Sephardim are descendants of the Jews of Spain and Portugal.

cards.front: When were the Jews expelled from Spain?
Who founded Chasidism?
cards.back: Israel Baal Shem Tov (c. 1698–1760).

cards.front: How many Jews perished in the Shoah?
cards.back: About six million, a third of the people.

cards.front: When is Yom HaShoah observed?
cards.back: On 27 Nisan.

cards.front: When was the State of Israel proclaimed?
cards.back: May 14, 1948 (5 Iyar 5708), by David Ben-Gurion.

cards.front: Who convened the First Zionist Congress, and where?
cards.back: Theodor Herzl, Basel, 1897.

cards.front: What does the Pesach Haggadah require of every Jew?
cards.back: To see himself as if he himself had come out of Egypt.

cards.front: Where does the word “Jew” (*Yehudi*) come from?
cards.back: From the tribe of Yehudah (Judah).

cards.front: When was the Second Temple dedicated?
cards.back: Around 516 BCE. Cyrus permitted the return from exile in 538 BCE.

cards.front: Who was the first king of Israel?
cards.back: Shaul (Saul); after him came David, and then Shlomo.

cards.front: What did Ezra and Nechemiah do after the return from Babylonia?
cards.back: They restored life according to the Torah.

cards.front: How did the Bar Kochba revolt (132–135) end?
cards.back: It was brutally crushed; Rabbi Akiva was killed; Jews were forbidden to enter Jerusalem.

cards.front: Who are the Mitnagdim?
cards.back: Opponents of Chasidism, led by the Vilna Gaon; they developed the scholarship of the Lithuanian yeshivot.

cards.front: What is the Kotel?
cards.back: The Western Wall, a remnant of the wall surrounding the Temple Mount; a place of Jewish prayer.

cards.front: What is Jerusalem for the Jewish people?
cards.back: Its eternal and undivided capital; in 1967 the city was reunited, and Jews returned to the Kotel.

cards.front: How does this course suggest relating to the State of Israel?
cards.back: As the return of the people to its Land and as a reason for thanksgiving; Yom HaAtzmaut is a Jewish day of joy.

lessons.title: The 613 Commandments and the Seven Laws of the Descendants of Noach
citations: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 8:11
keyIdeas: Jewish life is built around mitzvot; according to tradition there are 613: 248 positive and 365 negative commandments.
Commandments “between a person and G-d” and “between a person and his fellow” are equally commanded.
Yom Kippur does not atone for sins against one’s fellow without reconciling with him (Mishnah Yoma 8:9).
“Love your fellow as yourself” is a great principle of the Torah (R. Akiva); Hillel: “What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow.”
For the sake of pikuach nefesh almost any commandment is set aside; the seven Noahide laws are for all humanity, and a righteous non-Jew is close to G-d.

blocks.text: What Is a Mitzvah
a commandment, an instruction from G-d (pl. *mitzvot*). In everyday speech any good deed is also called a “mitzvah,” but in the precise sense it is an obligation imposed by the Torah or by the sages.

Jewish life is built around mitzvot. They sanctify ordinary actions (eating, sleeping, working, family life), turning them into service. Before performing many commandments, Jews recite a blessing: “…who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us…”. In this sense a mitzvah is not a burden but a way of being in constant connection with the Almighty.
The Number 613

The Talmud records the words of Rabbi Simlai: “613 commandments were stated to Moshe: 365 negative commandments, corresponding to the number of days in the solar year, and 248 positive commandments, corresponding to the number of organs (limbs) of the human body” (Makkot 23b). The sages saw a symbol in this: every day a person must guard against evil, and with every part of the body serve G-d. In Hebrew the number 613 is written with the letters **TARYAG** (תַּרְיַ״ג), which is why people speak of “taryag mitzvot.”

items: **Mitzvot aseh** (מִצְווֹת עֲשֵׂה): positive commandments, “do”: for example, reciting the Shema, putting on tefillin, sanctifying Shabbat, tzedakah.
**Mitzvot lo ta’aseh** (מִצְווֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה): negative commandments, “do not”: for example, do not steal, do not eat non-kosher food, do not work on Shabbat.

blocks.text: The Torah itself contains no exact list of the 613 commandments. Various authorities compiled such lists; the best known is in Rambam’s “Book of the Commandments” (*Sefer HaMitzvot*), which also opens his Mishneh Torah. Many commandments cannot be fulfilled today: they are connected with the Temple and the sacrifices, with the Land of Israel in the Temple era, or with a Jewish king and the Sanhedrin. Some commandments apply only to kohanim, only to men or only to women. So each person fulfills only part of the 613, but together the people keeps the whole Torah.

Besides the commandments of the Torah (*de’oraita*), there are commandments instituted by the sages (*derabbanan*): for example, lighting Chanukah candles, reading Megillat Esther on Purim, washing the hands before a meal with bread, blessings before eating, and lighting Shabbat candles. Halacha takes them seriously but distinguishes in strictness: in a case of doubt about a Torah law one is stringent, and in a case of doubt about a rabbinic law one is lenient.
Between a Person and G-d, Between a Person and a Person

The sages divide the commandments into two large groups: **bein adam laMakom**, “between a person and the Almighty” (prayer, Shabbat, kashrut, festivals), and **bein adam lechavero**, “between a person and his fellow” (honesty in business, tzedakah, the prohibition of evil speech, honoring parents, caring for the ger, the widow and the orphan). Both groups are equally commanded. The Ten Commandments were written on two tablets, and according to the traditional explanation the first tablet is devoted to our relationship with G-d and the second to our relationships with people.

The Mishnah teaches: Yom Kippur atones for sins between a person and G-d, but for sins between a person and his fellow it does not atone until the person has appeased the one he wronged (Yoma 8:9). One cannot be “religious” at the expense of one’s fellow.

blocks.translit: Ve’ahavta lere’acha kamocha, ani Adonai
blocks.ru: Love your fellow as yourself: I am Hashem

blocks.text: Rabbi Akiva called this verse “a great principle of the Torah” (Sifra, Kedoshim). And Hillel, answering a non-Jew who came to convert, put it this way:

blocks.he: דַּעֲלָךְ סְנֵי לְחַבְרָךְ לָא תַּעֲבֵיד — זוֹ הִיא כָּל הַתּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ, וְאִידַךְ פֵּירוּשָׁהּ הוּא, זִיל גְּמוֹר
blocks.translit: Da’alach sni lechavrach la ta’avid — zo hi kol haTorah kulah, ve’idach perushah hu, zil gmor
blocks.ru: What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow: this is the whole Torah, the rest is commentary; go and learn

blocks.text: Note the ending: “go and learn.” Hillel did not say that the ritual commandments are unimportant; he gave the foundation on which the study and fulfillment of the whole Torah is built.
The world stands on three things: on Torah, on service (of G-d) and on acts of kindness.
Life Comes Before Almost Everything

Of the commandments it is said: “…which a person shall do and live by them” (Vayikra 18:5). The sages derive from this: “live by them, and not die because of them” (Yoma 85b). Therefore, to save a life (*pikuach nefesh*), almost any commandment is set aside, including Shabbat and the Yom Kippur fast. There are only three exceptions, for which one must rather die than transgress: idolatry, forbidden relations (incest and adultery) and murder (Sanhedrin 74a).
The Seven Laws of the Descendants of Noach
Judaism does not hold that every person must become a Jew. According to the Talmud, all humanity, the descendants of Noach (*bnei Noach*), are bound by seven laws (Sanhedrin 56a):

items: Establish courts and just laws (*dinim*).
Do not blaspheme.
Do not worship idols.
Do not engage in forbidden relations.
Do not murder.
Do not steal.
Do not eat flesh torn from a living animal (*ever min hachai*).

blocks.text: Rambam writes that the righteous of the nations of the world who keep these laws have a share in the World to Come (Laws of Kings 8:11). This leads to an important conclusion for every candidate: giyur is not needed to “save one’s soul,” since a righteous non-Jew is also close to G-d. Giyur is a choice to take on *more*: to enter the covenant of Israel with all its 613 commandments, with all the responsibility and history of the people. That is exactly why Judaism does not engage in missionary activity, and why the beit din asks: “Why do you want this?”
Be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one, for you do not know the reward for the commandments.

The movements understand the binding nature of the mitzvot differently. For Orthodoxy and Masorti the commandments are binding, though Masorti allows halacha to develop through the decisions of its rabbinic bodies. Reform Judaism emphasizes the ethical commandments as the eternal core, while a person chooses the ritual commandments consciously, after study (“informed choice”).

differs.text: In Reform Judaism the ritual mitzvot are not considered unconditionally binding: the community and each individual take them on through informed choice, while the ethical commandments are the foundation.

lessons.title: Movements in Judaism Today
keyIdeas: The movements arose after the Emancipation and the Haskalah; the main difference between them is how they understand revelation and the binding nature of halacha.
Orthodoxy: Torah from Heaven and binding halacha; within it are the Litvaks, Chasidim, Modern Orthodoxy, Religious Zionism and Sephardi Orthodoxy.
Masorti holds halacha to be binding but evolving; decisions are made by the CJLS committee.
Reform: the Torah is an inspired testimony of the encounter with G-d, written down by people; the emphasis is on prophetic ethics and personal choice.
The movements’ conversions are recognized differently, but Jews of all movements are one people; respect for another’s path is part of Jewish ethics.

blocks.text: Where the Movements Came From

Until the end of the 18th century, almost all Jews lived within a single traditional Judaism: it had its debates, Ashkenazi and Sephardi customs, Chasidim and their opponents, but halacha was considered binding on everyone. Everything changed with **Emancipation** — Jews receiving civil rights in Western Europe — and with the **Haskalah** (the Jewish Enlightenment). Jews entered European society, universities and professions, and a question arose: how can Judaism be preserved in the modern world? The different answers to this question became the movements.

What chiefly separates the movements is their understanding of **revelation** (how exactly G-d gave the Torah) and, as a consequence, of **the binding nature of halacha**. Below is an honest overview of how each movement sees itself.
Orthodox Judaism

Orthodoxy holds that the Written and Oral Torah were given by G-d to Moshe at Sinai (*Torah min ha-shamayim* — “Torah from Heaven”), and that halacha, as set out in the Talmud and the Shulchan Aruch, remains binding today. Halacha can be applied to new circumstances (electricity, medicine, technology), but decisions are made by recognized Torah scholars on the basis of the classical sources. There are many groups within Orthodoxy:

items: **Litvaks** (the Lithuanian stream, *misnagdim*) — heirs of the Vilna Gaon; at the center of their life is in-depth study of the Talmud in yeshivot (one of the first was the yeshiva in Volozhin, founded in 1803 by Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin).

**Chasidim** — followers of the Baal Shem Tov; they emphasize joy, heartfelt prayer and serving G-d in everything; they are united around a rebbe, a spiritual leader. Well-known Chasidic movements: Chabad (Lubavitch), Satmar, Gur, Belz, Breslov Chasidim. Chabad is especially active in the countries of the former USSR.

**Modern Orthodoxy** — combines strict observance of halacha with participation in modern society, secular education and professions. Its roots are the principle of “Torah im derech eretz” (Torah together with the way of the world) of Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch (Germany, 19th century) and “Torah u-Madda” (Torah and science) of Yeshiva University in New York.
**Religious Zionism** — sees in the State of Israel the beginning of the Redemption; its spiritual father is Rav Avraham Yitzchak Kook, the first Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of the Land of Israel.
**Sephardi Orthodoxy** — follows the rulings of the Shulchan Aruch without the glosses of the Rema, and the traditions of the communities of the East (a great authority is Rav Ovadia Yosef).

blocks.text: Orthodox (especially Haredi, “ultra-Orthodox”) communities are also distinguished by their appearance: strictly modest clothing, head coverings for men, and covered hair for married women. Modern Orthodox Jews look varied, but they keep the same laws of Shabbat, kashrut and family purity.
Conservative Judaism (Masorti)

The Conservative movement grew out of the “Positive-Historical School” of Rabbi Zacharias Frankel (the Breslau Seminary, 1854). In the USA its center became the Jewish Theological Seminary (JTS, founded in 1886–1887), which rose to prominence under Solomon Schechter. Outside North America the movement is called **Masorti** (“traditional”). Masorti considers halacha *binding*, but sees it as a living system that has always developed and must continue to develop. Decisions are made by the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards of the Rabbinical Assembly (CJLS); sometimes it allows several well-founded opinions, and the community’s rabbi chooses between them.

In practice, Conservative Judaism requires observance of Shabbat and kashrut and prayer in Hebrew, but it does, for example, permit driving to the synagogue on Shabbat (a 1950 ruling), and since 1985 JTS has ordained women as rabbis. Masorti understands the Torah as revelation expressed through human transmission and history.
Reform (Progressive) Judaism

Reform began in Germany at the start of the 19th century (Israel Jacobson, the synagogue in Seesen, 1810; Rabbi Abraham Geiger). In the USA its leader was Rabbi Isaac Mayer Wise, who founded Hebrew Union College (1875). Today Reform and Progressive communities are united in the **World Union for Progressive Judaism** (WUPJ, founded in 1926); in Russia, the ROOPI communities belong to it. Reform Judaism sees the Torah as an inspired testimony of the people’s encounter with G-d, written down by human beings, and emphasizes the **ethical prophetic heritage** and **personal autonomy**: every Jew studies the tradition and makes an informed choice about which commandments to observe.

Reform introduced full equality of men and women (the first woman rabbi was Regina Jonas, Germany, 1935; in the USA, Sally Priesand, 1972), prayer in the vernacular alongside Hebrew, and, in the USA, recognition of Jewish descent through the father. Over time the Reform movement has brought back much of the tradition: more Hebrew, kippot and tallitot, attention to Shabbat and kashrut.

differs.text: From the point of view of Reform Judaism, the development and change of practice is not a departure but a continuation of the prophetic tradition: Judaism has always changed together with the life of the people.

blocks.text: There are other movements too: **Reconstructionism** (Rabbi Mordecai Kaplan, USA), which understands Judaism as the evolving civilization of the Jewish people, and secular Humanistic Judaism. Many Israelis call themselves *masortim* (traditional): they observe much, though not everything, without belonging to any movement.

The core of the Reform approach to the Torah and mitzvot is often called **conscious choice**. A person is not free simply to brush a commandment aside for convenience: they are obliged to study it, to hear the voice of the tradition, of the community and of their own conscience, and only then decide how to fulfill it in their life. For a Reform Jew, halacha is neither an empty quantity nor an enemy, but the accumulated wisdom of the generations, with which one conducts a serious conversation. The Central Conference of American Rabbis (CCAR) has published responsa and resolutions for well over a century; the World Union for Progressive Judaism (WUPJ) links communities from North America and Israel to Europe and the CIS.

From this also come the equality of men and women in community life, openness to gerim and to those who have come by a difficult road, attention to tikkun olam as a religious and not merely civic task, and a readiness to revise established practices if, in the movement’s view, they no longer serve justice and human dignity. This is a path of its own within the Jewish people, not “Orthodoxy lite”. A candidate going before a Reform beit din should be able to explain this path in their own words — just as confidently as an Orthodox candidate explains the binding nature of halacha.
The Movements and Giyur

items: **Orthodox giyur:** acceptance of all the commandments, brit milah (or hatafat dam brit) for men, and tevilah are required; a beit din of three observant judges; the candidate usually lives in the community, keeping Shabbat and kashrut. It is recognized by all movements.
**Conservative giyur:** also brit milah, tevilah and a beit din of three, with acceptance of the commandments as Masorti understands them; it is recognized by Conservative and Reform communities.

**Reform giyur:** study, participation in community life, and acceptance of the Jewish destiny and of the commandments through informed choice; brit milah and tevilah are not required everywhere, but in many communities (in Israel, in the CIS countries) they are performed.

blocks.text: The Sages teach: “Every dispute for the sake of Heaven will endure in the end” (Avot 5:17), and of the disputes between the schools of Hillel and Shammai it is said: “These and those are the words of the living G-d” (Eruvin 13b). For all their differences, Jews of the various movements are one people. Respect for people on a different path is itself part of Jewish ethics.

At the beit din you may be asked why you chose this particular movement. A good answer does not say that “it’s easier there”, but speaks of which understanding of the Torah and which community feel close to you, and where you see your future Jewish life.

lessons.title: The Land of Israel, Zion and the State of Israel
citations: Ramban, glosses to “Sefer HaMitzvot”, positive commandment 4
Siddur, the Amidah: the blessings for the ingathering of the exiles and for Jerusalem
keyIdeas: The Land of Israel was given to the people by an eternal covenant (Bereshit 17:8); Jerusalem is the eternal and undivided capital.
In exile, Jews prayed every day for the return; love of Zion and aliyah are part of Jewish life.
The State of Israel (5 Iyar 5708 / May 14, 1948) is the return of the people to its Land; Yom HaAtzmaut is a day of thanksgiving.
Yom Yerushalayim marks the reunification of Jerusalem in 1967; Yom HaZikaron remembers those who fell for the Land and the people.
In all the movements covered by this course, loyalty to the Land and to Israel is part of the Jewish path, not an “optional view”.

blocks.text: The Land of the Covenant

Jewish history begins not only with the word and the commandment, but also with the Land. The Almighty says to Avraham: “To your descendants I will give this land” (Bereshit 12:7). Later the covenant is described in all its fullness: “To your descendants I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates (Perat)” (Bereshit 15:18). And again: “And I will give to you and to your descendants after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession” (Bereshit 17:8). This is not a temporary agreement and not a “disputed territory”: Eretz Israel in all its fullness is the land of the Jewish people by an eternal covenant.
A land which Hashem your G-d cares for: the eyes of Hashem your G-d are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year.

The Torah praises this land as a land “of wheat and barley, of vines, figs and pomegranates, a land of olive trees and honey” (Devarim 8:8) and commands us to bless G-d for it after eating (Devarim 8:10). The heart of the Land is Jerusalem, the city of the Temple and of David’s kingdom. For a Jew it is not divided and never ceases to be the capital: it is the eternal and undivided capital of the people of Israel. Yehuda and Shomron, the Golan and Aza are part of the memory and the map of this Land; the Hebrew names of places here are not decoration but the language of the Torah and the prophets themselves.
The Prayer of Exile and the Return

After the destruction of the Temples, the people lived in exile but did not forget the Land. Three times a day, in the standing prayer, the Amidah, a Jew asks for the ingathering of the exiles and says: “And to Jerusalem, Your city, return in mercy… and speedily establish the throne of David within it.” On Pesach and on Yom Kippur we hear “L’shanah haba’ah bi-Yerushalayim” — “Next year in Jerusalem”. The psalm sung by the rivers of Babylon became the measure of memory:

blocks.translit: Im eshkachech Yerushalayim, tishkach yemini
blocks.ru: If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget

blocks.text: The Ramban counts settling the Land of Israel as a Torah commandment for all generations (glosses to the Rambam’s “Sefer HaMitzvot”, positive commandment 4). The Rambam writes that it is better for a person to live in the Land of Israel, even in a city whose majority is not Jewish, than outside it in a city whose majority is Jewish, and that one should leave the Land only for a serious reason (Laws of Kings 5:9–12). Even someone who for now lives in the Diaspora turns their face toward Jerusalem and carries the Land in prayer, in study and in caring for the people who live there.

Aliyah — “going up” to the Land of Israel — becomes for many families a living continuation of this prayer. The beit din should not hear that you need giyur “for the paperwork”; but love of the Land, the wish to live in it or to support it, is a natural and welcome part of the Jewish path.
The State of Israel

The dream of returning to Zion was never just poetry. At the end of the 19th century, political Zionism gave this dream the form of a state: Theodor Herzl convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel (1897). On **May 14, 1948** (5 Iyar 5708), David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the **State of Israel**. For the first time in almost two thousand years, the people once again had its own state in its own Land. This day is celebrated as **Yom HaAtzmaut** — a day of thanksgiving, not an “optional date on the calendar”.

The Law of Return (1950) opened the way home to every Jew, including those who have undergone giyur. In 1967, in the Six-Day War, Jerusalem was reunified, and Jews could once again pray at the Kotel. **Yom Yerushalayim**, on 28 Iyar, preserves this memory. On the eve of Yom HaAtzmaut the whole people observes **Yom HaZikaron** — the day of remembrance for fallen soldiers and victims of terror: the joy of independence stands beside the price that was paid for it.
Behold, I will open your graves and bring you up out of your graves, O My people, and bring you into the land of Israel.

The State of Israel is the return of the people to its Land, the beginning of the fulfillment of the prayer of generations. At the same time, the complete redemption spoken of in the twelfth principle is still ahead: the Temple has not been rebuilt, and Judaism still awaits Mashiach. One does not cancel the other: we can give thanks for what has already happened and await what has been promised.
How the movements see it

The early Reform platform in Pittsburgh (1885) still held back from a political return to Zion. This was revised long ago: already the Columbus Platform (1937) and subsequent decisions of the CCAR and the WUPJ unequivocally bind Reform Judaism to love of the Land and to support for the State of Israel. Today Progressive communities in Israel and in the Diaspora celebrate Yom HaAtzmaut and Yom Yerushalayim and see Israel as the homeland of the Jewish people.

The Conservative movement (Masorti) has been bound up with Zion from the very beginning; its siddurim contain special prayers for these days, and the Masorti movement is active in Israel. Orthodox Religious Zionism, in the tradition of Rav Kook, sees in the return of the people the beginning of the redemption and recites Hallel on these days. In some communities the liturgy on Yom HaAtzmaut is not changed; yet love of the Land and responsibility for the people who live in it do not thereby become “optional”. In all three paths of this course, loyalty to Eretz Israel and to the State of Israel is part of what it means to be a Jew.

At the beit din you may be asked: “What does Israel mean to you?” Answer calmly and in your own words: it is the Land of the covenant, Jerusalem is the eternal capital, the people has come home, and I want to be part of this story. Don’t reduce your answer to politics alone, and don’t make “immigration papers” the main reason for your giyur — but don’t hide your love of the Land either, as if it were something superfluous.

cards.front: To whom, and on what terms, does the Torah promise the Land of Israel?
cards.back: To the descendants of Avraham, as an everlasting possession (Bereshit 12:7; 17:8). It is the land of the covenant, not a temporary gift.

cards.front: What borders of the land are named in Bereshit 15:18?
cards.back: “From the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates (Perat).” The Torah describes the Land in all its fullness.

cards.front: What does Jerusalem mean for a Jew?
cards.back: The eternal and undivided capital of the people, the city of the Temple and of prayer; “If I forget you, Jerusalem…” (Tehillim 137:5).

cards.front: What do we ask for in the Amidah when speaking of the Land?
cards.back: For the ingathering of the exiles, for the return to Jerusalem and for the throne of David.

cards.front: What does “L'shanah haba'ah bi-Yerushalayim” mean?
cards.back: “Next year in Jerusalem”: words said on Pesach and on Yom Kippur.

cards.front: How does the Ramban view settling the Land of Israel?
cards.back: As a Torah commandment for all generations (Additions to Sefer HaMitzvot, positive commandment 4).

cards.front: What does the Rambam advise about where to live (Laws of Kings 5:9–12)?
cards.back: It is better to live in the Land of Israel; leave it only for a serious reason.

cards.front: When was the State of Israel proclaimed?
cards.back: May 14, 1948, 5 Iyar 5708; this day is celebrated as Yom HaAtzmaut.

cards.front: What is aliyah?
cards.back: Ascent: immigration, a return to live in the Land of Israel. The Law of Return (1950) opens this path to a ger as well.

cards.front: What is remembered on Yom Yerushalayim?
cards.back: 28 Iyar: the reunification of Jerusalem in 1967 and the return to the Kotel.

cards.front: Why does Yom HaZikaron come right before Yom HaAtzmaut?
cards.back: To remember the price of independence: the fallen soldiers and the victims of terror.

cards.front: Does the State of Israel cancel the waiting for Mashiach?
cards.back: No. The people have returned to their Land, and we give thanks for that; the complete redemption and the Temple are still ahead.

cards.front: How does Reform Judaism relate to Israel today?
cards.back: Having revised its early platform of 1885, the movement supports the State of Israel and celebrates Yom HaAtzmaut.

cards.front: Is love for the Land an “optional opinion” in Judaism?
cards.back: No. In all the movements covered in this course, loyalty to Eretz Israel and to Israel is part of the Jewish path.

cards.front: How should you speak about the Land at the beit din?
cards.back: In your own words: the Land of the covenant, Jerusalem as the eternal capital, a people that has come home. Don't reduce giyur to “paperwork.”

lessons.title: How to Read the Tanakh: Context, Hebrew and a Living Community
keyIdeas: A verse of the Tanakh is read in Hebrew, within its chapter and together with the tradition, not as a fragment torn out of its context.
The Oral Torah and the sages explain how to live by the Written Torah; “just the letters, without the sages” is not the way of Judaism.
Verses that are often reinterpreted: Yeshayahu 7:14 and 53, Tehillim 22 and 110, Daniel 9, Yirmiyahu 31, Michah 5:1, Zechariah 12:10.
A kippah, a holiday and a Hebrew name do not by themselves make a teaching Jewish.
Before joining a new community, ask a rabbi and check whether one of the established movements recognizes it.

blocks.text: Reading with your own eyes

The Tanakh is the book of the Jewish people, and it is read the way a living book is read: in Hebrew, as a whole, in connection with the surrounding verses and together with the tradition that has preserved the meaning of its words. A single verse, taken out of its chapter and translated so as to confirm a ready-made conclusion, can easily come to mean something that is not in it. That is why, throughout this course, we stop again and again and ask: what does the text itself say? Who is speaking? About whom? At what time? How did the sages understand it?

The Oral Torah here is neither an “add-on” nor a rival of the Written Torah. Without it, you cannot know how to perform almost any commandment: what counts as work on Shabbat, how tefillin are written, how shechitah is done. Groups that say, “The written lines alone are enough for us; we can bypass the sages,” in fact cut Judaism off from the way the people have always lived by the Torah. Curiously, the same groups often wear a kippah, light Shabbat candles and call their teacher a “rabbi,” and all of this comes precisely from the tradition of the sages that they reject.
Everything that I command you, take care to do it; do not add to it and do not take away from it.

The Torah warns of something else as well: even if a person gives a sign and it comes true, but he calls on you to serve differently from what the Almighty commanded, “do not listen to him… for the Lord is testing you” (Devarim 13:2–4). The Rambam applies this also to anyone who announces that the commandments of the Torah have been abolished or replaced (Foundations of the Torah 9:1–3). A miracle and eloquent speech do not cancel the Torah.
Verses that are often taken out of their chapter

Below are several passages that are often shown to a giyur candidate “as proof” of a redeemer who has already come, of a “composite” G-d, or of the Torah being replaced. The Jewish answer is short: read them yourself, in Hebrew and in context.

items: **“The young woman shall conceive” (Yeshayahu 7:14).** In Hebrew, *almah* means “young woman,” not a special word for a virgin. The sign was given to King Achaz in his own time: “before the boy learns to reject evil… the land will be abandoned” of the two hostile kings (Yeshayahu 7:16).

**“The servant of the Lord” (Yeshayahu 52:13–53:12).** The prophet himself calls the people the servant: “You are My servant, Israel” (Yeshayahu 49:3; 41:8). This is also how Rashi reads the chapter: it speaks of the people of Israel, who suffered among the nations and will be vindicated.

**Tehillim 22.** This is David's lament. In verse 22:17 the Hebrew text has *ka-ari*, “like a lion (they maul) my hands and my feet,” not the verb “they pierced.” The psalm ends with praise in the assembly of Israel, not with a scene of execution.

**Tehillim 110:1.** “The Lord said to my master (*la-adoni*).” The Hebrew here is *adoni*, “my master,” a way of addressing a human being, not the Divine Name *Adonai*. Rashi applies the psalm to Avraham; others read it as speaking of a king from the house of David. It is not a second “divine figure.”

**Daniel 9:24–27.** In Jewish tradition the “seventy weeks [of years]” speak of the period from the destruction of the First Temple, through the era of the Second, up to its destruction (so Rashi). It is not a timetable proving that Mashiach has already come.

**Yirmiyahu 31:30–32.** The “new covenant” (*brit chadashah*) is the same Torah, now written on the heart of Israel and Yehudah: “I will put My Torah within them and write it on their hearts.” The covenant does not cancel the Torah and does not transfer the covenant to another people.

**“Elohim” in the plural (Bereshit 1:1).** This is a form of majesty; the verb is in the singular: “In the beginning G-d created (*bara*).” The Torah can use the same word for a single human being (Shemot 7:1).

**Michah 5:1.** This speaks of a ruler from Beit Lechem Efratah, of the line of David: a human leader from an ancient lineage, from a humble town of Yehudah. “Whose origin is from of old” refers to the antiquity of his lineage, not to his being G-d Himself.

**Zechariah 12:10.** The people will mourn in Jerusalem “as one mourns for an only son.” The commentators apply this to those who fell in war or to a human redeemer from the house of Yosef who will die in battle. The verse does not say that G-d Himself was “pierced.”

blocks.text: What does not change in the teaching itself

These readings agree with what has already been said in the lessons on the Shema, on the Rambam's principles and on Mashiach. G-d is One, does not consist of “persons” and does not become a human being. Mashiach is a human being from the house of David, and he will be recognized by deeds completed in this world: the Temple, the ingathering of the exiles, peace, Torah. As long as this has not happened, he has not yet come, and there is no “second coming” in Judaism. The Torah is eternal: it is not replaced by a new covenant that would abolish the commandments. Forgiveness comes through teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah; “instead of bulls, the words of our lips” (Hoshea 14:3), and “the son shall not bear the guilt of the father” (Yechezkel 18:20). A person has a *yetzer hatov* and a *yetzer hara*, inclinations toward good and toward evil, but there is no inborn guilt that only an intermediary could remove.
How to recognize a living Jewish community

Judaism lives not only in books but in a community, with a rabbi, in a recognized beit din. Sometimes you come across a gathering that looks very “Jewish”: a kippah, a tallit, a menorah, holidays, Hebrew names, even a Torah scroll, and yet it teaches that G-d became a human being, that Mashiach has already come or that the Torah has already been replaced. Outward signs do not by themselves make a teaching Jewish. A resolution of the Central Conference of American Rabbis (CCAR, 1985) states what all the recognized movements agree on: such groups are not a movement of Judaism, even if they call themselves a synagogue and their leader a rabbi.

items: Ask directly: what is believed here about G-d, about Mashiach and about the Torah? An evasive answer is already a signal to look further.
Find out whether one of the established movements, Orthodox, Conservative (Masorti) or Reform, recognizes the community, and who ordained the rabbi.
Warmth, a free holiday meal or help in a difficult moment do not replace this check: kindness does not prove a teaching.

If you are in doubt, don't argue on your own and don't decide “by beautiful words.” Turn to your rabbi or your beit din: the fact that you don't have a ready answer does not mean the other person is right.

blocks.text: At the beit din you may be asked how you now understand G-d, Mashiach and the Torah, and what you will do if you meet a teaching that looks Jewish but says something else. Answer calmly: “I read the Tanakh in context and with the teachers of my community; a kippah and a holiday are not proof to me in themselves; if a doubt arises, I will go to my rabbi.”

cards.front: How does Judaism teach you to read a verse of the Tanakh?
cards.back: In Hebrew, within its chapter and together with the tradition, not as a fragment taken out of context for the sake of a ready-made conclusion.

cards.front: Why can't you make do with the Written Torah alone, without the sages?
cards.back: Without the Oral Torah, it is unknown how to perform the commandments. “Just the letters, without the sages” is not the way of Judaism.

cards.front: What does “almah” mean in Yeshayahu 7:14?
cards.back: “Young woman.” The sign was given to King Achaz in his own time, not as a description of a distant miracle.

cards.front: According to the Jewish reading, who is “the servant of the Lord” in Yeshayahu 53?
cards.back: The people of Israel: “You are My servant, Israel” (Yeshayahu 49:3; 41:8). Rashi reads it this way too.

cards.front: What does the Hebrew say in Tehillim 22:17?
cards.back: *Ka-ari*: “like a lion (they maul) my hands and my feet,” not the verb “they pierced.” It is David's lament.

cards.front: How does *adoni* in Tehillim 110:1 differ from *Adonai*?
cards.back: *Adoni* means “my master,” a way of addressing a human being. It is not the Divine Name and not a “second person” of G-d.

cards.front: According to Rashi, what period does Daniel 9 speak of?
cards.back: The time from the destruction of the First Temple, through the era of the Second, up to its destruction, not about Mashiach having already come.

cards.front: What is the “new covenant” in Yirmiyahu 31:30–32?
cards.back: The same Torah, written on the heart of Israel. The covenant does not cancel the commandments and is not transferred to another people.

cards.front: Why does “Elohim” not mean “several gods”?
cards.back: It is a form of majesty; the verb in Bereshit 1:1 is in the singular: *bara*.

cards.front: Whom does Michah 5:1 speak of as a ruler from Beit Lechem?
cards.back: A human leader from the line of David. “Origin from of old” refers to the antiquity of the lineage, not to a deity.

cards.front: How do Jewish commentators read Zechariah 12:10?
cards.back: As mourning for the fallen or for a human redeemer who will die in battle. Not as saying that G-d was “pierced.”

cards.front: Do a kippah, a tallit and a Hebrew name make a teaching Jewish?
cards.back: No. A teaching is recognized by what it says about G-d, Mashiach and the Torah, not by clothing and a name.

cards.front: What should you check before joining a new “synagogue”?
cards.back: What is believed about G-d, Mashiach and the Torah; whether one of the established movements recognizes the community; who ordained the rabbi.

cards.front: What should you do if you don't know the teaching well and the other person sounds confident?
cards.back: Don't argue on your own. Your not having an answer does not prove they are right. Go to your rabbi.

cards.front: Does a miracle or a “sign that came true” cancel the Torah?
cards.back: No. Devarim 13:2–4 and the Rambam (Foundations of the Torah 9:1–3): even a sign gives no right to abolish the commandments.

A ger toshav underwent giyur in Israel; a ger tzedek underwent giyur abroad

For me this is a decision about my life and the lives of my future children.

questions.explanation: The reverse: the Pharisees accepted the Oral Torah, while the Sadducees recognized only the Written Torah.

questions.explanation: The main milestones in the codification of halacha.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows the need for the Oral Torah?
options: The Torah commands wearing “totafot” but doesn't explain what they are (tefillin)
The Torah tells the story of the creation of the world
The Torah contains the Ten Commandments
The Torah gives the names of the forefathers

questions.prompt: Explain what the Oral Torah is and why Judaism considers it necessary.
questions.modelAnswer: The Oral Torah is the interpretation and the laws that, according to tradition, Moshe received at Sinai together with the Written Torah and handed down through a chain of generations: to Yehoshua, the elders, the prophets and the Men of the Great Assembly (Avot 1:1). Without it, many commandments cannot be fulfilled: the Torah speaks of “totafot,” of shechitah “as I have commanded you,” of the prohibition of work on Shabbat, but it does not give the details. Around 200 CE it was written down in the Mishnah; then the discussions of the sages went into the Gemara, and together they make up the Talmud. Later, the codes were built on them: the Rambam's Mishneh Torah and the Shulchan Aruch.

The chain of transmission (Avot 1:1)
Examples: tefillin, shechitah, the melachot of Shabbat
Mishnah → Gemara → Talmud
The codes of halacha

As belief in the imminent coming of a king from the house of David
As a rejection of any hope for the future
As belief in a Mashiach from the line of Aharon

questions.prompt: Name the foundations of Jewish faith according to the Rambam, grouping them, and say which principle is especially close to you and why.
questions.modelAnswer: The Rambam lists 13 principles. The first five are about G-d: He exists and created everything, He is One, incorporeal and eternal, and one may pray only to Him. Principles 6–9 are about prophecy and the Torah: G-d speaks through prophets, Moshe is the greatest prophet, the Torah was given to Moshe and will not be replaced. The last four are about Divine providence and the future: G-d knows people's deeds, rewards and punishes, Mashiach will come, and there will be the resurrection of the dead. The principle of G-d's unity is especially close to me; I say it every day in the Shema. It means that the whole world and my whole life have one Source and one meaning.

Group 1–5: about G-d
Group 6–9: prophecy and the Torah
Group 10–13: judgment, Mashiach, resurrection
Personal explanation

“In the beginning G-d created the heaven and the earth” (Bereshit 1:1)

questions.prompt: What does it mean that the Jews are the “chosen people”? Do you think this is arrogance?
questions.modelAnswer: Chosenness in Judaism is not superiority but a task and a responsibility. The Torah says outright that G-d chose Israel not because it was larger or better than others (Devarim 7:7–8), and the prophet Amos adds: “You alone have I known… therefore I will visit upon you” (Amos 3:2). Israel is called to be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Shemot 19:6) and “a light unto the nations” (Yeshayahu 42:6) — to live by the Torah and show the world the path of justice. Chosenness is not racial: anyone can join through giyur, and the righteous of other nations are also close to G-d.

questions.explanation: Yavneh became the center of Torah study after the destruction of the Temple.
questions.source: Gittin 56b

questions.prompt: What is the Hebrew name for the catastrophe of European Jewry (one word)?
questions.explanation: Shoah — the Catastrophe; about six million murdered.
questions.source: EJE, article “The Catastrophe”

questions.prompt: A beit din member says: “The Jewish people has suffered greatly and still faces antisemitism today. Are you ready to share this fate?” Answer.
questions.modelAnswer: I understand that by accepting giyur I am joining not only a faith but the history of a people — the Exodus and Sinai, the destruction of the two Temples, two thousand years of exile, the Shoah in which six million perished, and the rebirth of the State of Israel. The Talmud requires asking this question of the candidate, and I answer as Rut did: “your people shall be my people.” I am ready to share this fate, because I see in it not only suffering but the faithfulness to the covenant that has preserved the people. My future children will be Jews, and I want to pass this history on to them with pride.
keyPoints: Understanding the history of suffering and rebirth
Yevamot 47a — this question is asked of the candidate
Ruth 1:16
Fidelity to the covenant
Responsibility for future children
questions.explanation: The question tests seriousness and freedom of choice.
questions.source: Yevamot 47a; Rut 1:16

questions.prompt: How many positive and negative commandments are there in the Torah according to Makkot 23b?
questions.explanation: 248 — corresponding to the limbs of the body, 365 — to the days of the solar year.
questions.source: Makkot 23b

questions.prompt: Which of these laws is NOT among the Seven Noahide Laws?
questions.explanation: Shabbat is a commandment for Jews; the Seven Noahide Laws are listed in Sanhedrin 56a.
questions.source: Sanhedrin 56a

questions.prompt: Yom Kippur by itself atones for a person's sins against others.
questions.explanation: You must first appease the injured party (Mishnah Yoma 8:9).
questions.source: Mishnah Yoma 8:9

questions.prompt: Which prohibition may NOT be violated even to save a life?
questions.explanation: Three exceptions: idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, murder.
questions.source: Sanhedrin 74a

questions.prompt: What did Hillel answer the non-Jew who asked to be taught the whole Torah “while standing on one foot”?
options: “What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow; the rest is commentary — go and learn”
“Keep Shabbat — and that is the whole Torah”
questions.explanation: Hillel's answer is the foundation; “go and learn” implies studying the whole Torah. It was Shammai who turned this man away.
questions.source: Shabbat 31a

questions.prompt: According to the Rambam, the righteous of the nations of the world who keep the Seven Noahide Laws have a share in the World to Come.
questions.explanation: Laws of Kings 8:11.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 8:11

questions.prompt: Tell about the division of the commandments into “between a person and G-d” and “between a person and his fellow.” Which of them are more important?
questions.modelAnswer: The sages divide the commandments into “bein adam la-Makom” — between a person and the Almighty (prayer, Shabbat, kashrut) — and “bein adam le-chavero” — between a person and his fellow (honesty, tzedakah, the prohibition of gossip). Both groups were commanded by the one G-d and are equally binding; even the Ten Commandments are divided into two tablets. The Mishnah teaches that Yom Kippur does not atone for sins against one's fellow until the person makes peace with the injured party (Yoma 8:9). Hillel said: “What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow — that is the whole Torah,” but he added: “go and learn,” meaning that ethics is the foundation of the whole Torah, not a replacement for ritual.
keyPoints: Two kinds of commandments with examples
Both are binding
Mishnah Yoma 8:9
Hillel, Shabbat 31a
Vayikra 19:18
questions.explanation: You need to show the balance of ritual and ethics.
questions.source: Mishnah Yoma 8:9; Shabbat 31a; Vayikra 19:18

questions.prompt: What is the saving of a life, for the sake of which almost any commandment may be violated, called (two words)?
questions.explanation: “And he shall live by them” (Vayikra 18:5; Yoma 85b).
questions.source: Vayikra 18:5; Yoma 85b

questions.prompt: How does Conservative Judaism (Masorti) relate to halacha?
options: Halacha is binding, but develops historically
Halacha is not binding; personal choice decides everything
Halacha is unchanging and allows no new rulings
questions.explanation: Masorti holds halacha to be binding but evolving (rulings of the CJLS).
questions.source: Masorti: Rabbinical Assembly; EJE, article “Conservative Judaism”

questions.prompt: Whose principle “Torah im derech eretz” became the foundation of Modern Orthodoxy?
questions.explanation: Hirsch (Germany, 19th century) combined strict halacha with participation in modern society.
questions.source: EJE, article “Hirsch, Shimshon Raphael”

questions.prompt: Where and when did Reform Judaism arise?
options: In Germany in the early 19th century
questions.explanation: Israel Jacobson (Seesen, 1810), Avraham Geiger.
questions.source: EJE, article “Reform Judaism”

questions.prompt: Chabad is one of the Hasidic movements.
questions.explanation: Chabad (Lubavitch) is a Hasidic movement, very active in the countries of the former USSR.
questions.source: EJE, article “Chabad”

questions.prompt: A giyur of which movement is recognized by all movements of Judaism?
questions.explanation: An Orthodox giyur is recognized by all; non-Orthodox ones are not recognized by Orthodoxy.
questions.source: “Giyur in the Context of Different Denominations of Judaism” (CyberLeninka)

questions.prompt: Why did you choose this particular movement and this particular community for your giyur?
questions.modelAnswer: The answer builds on understanding the differences. Orthodoxy sees the Written and Oral Torah as a revelation from Sinai and considers halacha binding in its entirety. Masorti considers halacha binding but evolving, while Reform Judaism emphasizes ethics, autonomy, and informed choice. I chose this community because its understanding of the Torah is close to me, I take part in its life, pray and learn together with it, and I see the future of my family here. I understand how this beit din's giyur is recognized, and I respect Jews of other movements as part of one people.
keyPoints: Knowledge of the differences between the movements (revelation, halacha)
A positive reason for the choice, not “it's easier”
Participation in community life
Understanding the issues of recognition
Respect for other movements
questions.explanation: The beit din wants to see a conscious, informed choice.
questions.source: “Giyur in the Context of Various Denominations of Judaism” (CyberLeninka); Pirkei Avot 5:17

questions.prompt: How would you respond to someone who says: “Jews of different movements are different religions”?
questions.modelAnswer: The movements of Judaism understand revelation and the bindingness of halacha differently, and these differences are serious: recognition of giyur and marriage, for example, depends on them. But they all rely on one Torah, one history, and one covenant; they pray to the same G-d in the words of the Shema and consider themselves part of one people. The sages taught that a dispute “for the sake of Heaven” endures (Avot 5:17), and of the schools of Hillel and Shammai it is said: “both these and those are the words of the living G-d” (Eruvin 13b). Therefore I see in Jews of different movements one family with different views.
keyPoints: The differences are real (revelation, halacha, recognition of giyur)
A shared Torah, history, and people
Avot 5:17 — a dispute for the sake of Heaven
Eruvin 13b
Respect and the unity of the people
questions.explanation: Tests understanding and tact.
questions.source: Pirkei Avot 5:17; Eruvin 13b

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: read Rut's words “your people shall be my people, and your G-d my G-d” and explain what they mean to you personally. Why is the people mentioned before G-d?
questions.modelAnswer: These words of the Moabite Rut, spoken to her mother-in-law Naomi, are for me a brief description of my own path. I want to say the same: your people shall be my people, and your G-d my G-d. The order in the verse matters to me: first the people, with its history and fate, and only then faith and commandments. One without the other is incomplete. I am coming to both the people and G-d, as Rut did, and after giyur I will bind my life and the life of my future children to this people.
keyPoints: The formula from Rut 1:16
First the people, then faith and commandments — both are essential
Personal readiness to share the fate of the people
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate understands that giyur combines joining the people and accepting the faith, rather than substituting one for the other.
questions.source: Ruth 1:16

questions.prompt: The rabbi asks: The Mishnah says that Moshe received the Torah from Sinai and passed it on down the chain of generations. What does it mean for you to enter this chain of transmission?
questions.modelAnswer: The Mishnah in tractate Avot describes the chain: Moshe received the Torah from Sinai and passed it to Yehoshua, he to the elders, they to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly. For me, entering this chain means receiving the teaching that the community already safeguards, not inventing a tradition from scratch. It has reached us in the Mishnah, the Talmud, and the codes of halacha, and today the rabbis I learn from are bringing me into it. The Torah is the heritage of the whole community, not the property of scholars, so I want to study it and pass it on, including to my children.
keyPoints: The chain of transmission: Moshe, Yehoshua, the elders, the prophets, the Great Assembly (Avot 1:1)
To accept the community's teaching, not invent a tradition from scratch
The Torah is the heritage of the whole community; it is studied and passed on
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate understands that he is entering a tradition the people have already handed down from generation to generation.
questions.source: Pirkei Avot 1:1

differs.text: Reform Judaism sees the Torah and the Talmud as an inspired but humanly created heritage from which practice is chosen after study. Here the chain of transmission is the tradition of the community, not the bindingness of the whole halacha.

questions.prompt: At the beit din they ask: how do you personally understand the Rambam's last principles — the coming of the Mashiach and the resurrection of the dead? Do you believe in them literally?
questions.modelAnswer: The Rambam's twelfth principle is the coming of the Mashiach: according to tradition, this is a king from the descendants of David who will gather the exiles, rebuild the Temple, and bring the world peace and knowledge of G-d. The thirteenth is the resurrection of the dead, when the Creator so wills; it is spoken of in the second blessing of the Amidah: “You revive the dead.” The words “Ani Maamin” — “though he delays, I await him every day” — are, for me, the hope that history has an ending. I will not pretend that I have already lived this faith to the end: it calls me to study the Torah and do good, not to wait idly. To the question whether I believe this literally, I will answer without memorized phrases: I take the hope seriously and speak of it as my movement understands it.
keyPoints: Principle 12: the Mashiach from the descendants of David; principle 13: the resurrection of the dead
“Ani Maamin”: to wait for him every day, though he delays
An honest answer according to your own movement, without someone else's formula
questions.explanation: The beit din listens to whether the candidate understands what the principles about the Mashiach and resurrection mean and whether he speaks honestly about his faith.
questions.source: Rambam, Commentary to the Mishnah, Sanhedrin, ch. 10; Siddur: “Ani Maamin,” “Yigdal”

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, belief in a personal Mashiach is replaced by belief in a coming messianic age of peace and justice, which people bring nearer through their deeds; bodily resurrection is replaced by the immortality of the soul (Pittsburgh Platform, 1885).
Masorti allows different understandings of revelation (principles 8–9) and does not require a literal interpretation of principles 12–13 (statement “Emet ve-Emunah,” 1988).

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: what is the covenant between G-d and the people of Israel, and what does entering this covenant through giyur mean to you personally?
questions.modelAnswer: The covenant, brit, is the mutual commitments of G-d and the people. The sign of the covenant with Noah is the rainbow, with Avraham — brit milah, and at Sinai the whole people accepted the Torah. The people answered: “All that the L-rd has spoken, we will do and we will hear” — naaseh ve-nishma. The sages admire that “we will do” came before “we will hear”: they took on the commitment even before knowing all the details. For me, giyur is the same kind of step: I am ready to enter the covenant and accept the commandments, and my understanding will grow through study and life in the community.
keyPoints: Brit — the mutual commitments of G-d and the people
Signs of the covenant: the rainbow, brit milah, the Torah at Sinai
“Naaseh ve-nishma” (Shemot 24:7): “we will do” comes first
Readiness to enter the covenant; understanding grows through study
questions.explanation: The beit din looks at whether the candidate understands the covenant as mutual commitments and is ready to accept them, as the people did at Sinai.
questions.source: Shemot 24:7; Bereshit 17:7–10

questions.prompt: The rabbi asks: tell in your own words the main milestones of the history of the Jewish people — from Avraham to our days.
questions.modelAnswer: I understand that a ger accepts not only the faith but the history of the people. It begins with Avraham who, according to tradition, came on his own to faith in the one G-d, and continues with the Exodus from Egypt and the giving of the Torah at Sinai. Then come the kingdom of David and the First Temple of Shlomo, the destruction of the Temple in 586 BCE, the return under Cyrus, the Maccabean revolt and Chanukah. Then the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE and Yavneh, where the Torah was preserved, the long Diaspora — Ashkenazim, Sephardim, and the eastern communities, the Shoah in which about six million Jews perished, and the State of Israel in 1948. I will keep this memory through the holidays and pass it on to my children.
keyPoints: Milestones: Avraham, the Exodus, Sinai, the Temples, Yavneh, the Diaspora, the Shoah, the State of Israel
Understanding that the ger accepts the people's history in full
Memory through the holidays and passing it on to children
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate can retell the history of the people in his own words and understands that he accepts it together with the faith.
questions.source: ORT Electronic Jewish Encyclopedia (EEE)

questions.prompt: A beit din member asks: which commandments do you already try to keep in daily life? Give examples of “between a person and G-d” and “between a person and his fellow.”
questions.modelAnswer: I am at the beginning of the path and will not say that I already keep everything. Between a person and G-d, I try to read the Shema, I am learning the blessings before food, and step by step I am introducing Shabbat and kashrut as my community teaches. Between a person and his fellow, honesty, tzedakah, and care with speech — not speaking ill of others — matter to me. The Mishnah says that Yom Kippur does not atone for a wrong done to one's fellow until one makes peace with him, so these commandments are no less important to me than the ritual ones. A mitzvah, for me, is a way of remembering the Almighty in an ordinary act: in food, in work, and in conversation with people.
keyPoints: Examples from both groups, without claiming that everything is already observed
Yom Kippur does not replace making peace with one's fellow (Mishnah Yoma 8:9)
A mitzvah is a connection with the Almighty in everyday matters
Ritual — as one's own community teaches
questions.explanation: The beit din listens to the candidate's lived practice and to whether he understands that the commandments toward people are no less than the commandments toward G-d.
questions.source: Mishnah Yoma 8:9

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, ritual mitzvot are not unconditionally binding: they are adopted by informed choice, while the ethical commandments are the foundation. At the beit din, name what you have actually taken upon yourself.

questions.prompt: Who was Rut by origin, the model giyoret in the Tanakh?
questions.explanation: In the lesson, Rut is called a Moabite: after her husband's death she did not return to her people but joined the people of her mother-in-law.
questions.source: Lesson: Who Is a Jew and What Is Giyur

questions.prompt: What does the beit din ask a giyur candidate first, according to the Talmud (Yevamot 47a)?
options: Why do you want to live in the Land of Israel?
What did you see that made you come to accept giyur? Do you not know that the people of Israel are now oppressed and persecuted?
How many commandments of the Torah are you ready to keep every day?
questions.explanation: The beit din asks whether the candidate realizes that he is joining an oppressed and persecuted people — so that his decision is mature and free.
questions.source: Yevamot 47a

questions.prompt: What did the CCAR resolution of 1983 change in the Reform definition of who is a Jew?
options: It abolished the requirement of giyur for becoming Jewish
It prohibited brit milah in Reform communities
It recognized as Jewish a child of any Jewish parent when raised with a Jewish identity
It declared all Jewish giyurim equivalent
questions.explanation: The resolution introduced “patrilineal descent”: a child of a Jewish father is also recognized as Jewish if raised with a Jewish identity. Traditional halacha did not accept this definition.
questions.source: CCAR Resolution, 1983

differs.text: Masorti, like Orthodoxy, recognizes Jewishness only through the mother or through giyur; the child of a Jewish father and a non-Jewish mother needs giyur.

questions.prompt: According to the sages, what did the whole people of Israel “undergo” at Mount Sinai on the day the Torah was given?
options: A fast of three days and three nights
The circumcision of the whole people
questions.explanation: According to the sages, at Sinai the entire people themselves “underwent giyur”; therefore the book of Rut is read on Shavuot, the festival of the giving of the Torah.
questions.source: Lesson: Who Is a Jew and What Is Giyur

questions.prompt: The Torah forbids wronging a ger by word or deed and reminding him of his origins.
questions.explanation: The lesson says that a ger's past is no disgrace: the Torah forbids reminding him of his origin, and it directly forbids wronging him by word or deed (Shemot 22:20; Vayikra 19:33–34).
questions.source: Shemot 22:20; Vayikra 19:33–34

questions.prompt: According to one opinion in the Talmud, the Torah warns about treating the ger with care only three times.
questions.explanation: According to one opinion in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 59b), the Torah warns about the ger thirty-six times — to treat him with care.
questions.source: Bava Metzia 59b

questions.prompt: What is the symbolic drawing of a drop of blood called, performed instead of brit milah for a man who was circumcised before giyur?
questions.explanation: If a man is already circumcised, atafat dam brit — the symbolic drawing of a drop of blood — is performed instead of brit milah during giyur.
questions.source: Yevamot 46a–47b; Rambam, Laws of Forbidden Relations 13–14

questions.prompt: Match the concept from the topic of giyur with its meaning.
