pairs: A sacrifice brought at giyur, only while the Temple stood
The mitzvah to love the stranger
questions.explanation: Ruth was David's great-grandmother; the sacrifice at giyur was brought only in the era of the Temple; the Torah commands us to love the stranger; according to tradition, Shemaiah and Avtalyon descended from gerim.
questions.source: Lesson: Who Is a Jew and What Is Giyur

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: "Why were you initially dissuaded from giyur? What is this custom?" Answer.
questions.modelAnswer: I know that the beit din first dissuades the candidate — not to push him away, but so that the decision is free and serious. The Talmud (Yevamot 47a) says: the beit din asks the candidate what he saw that brought him, and warns him that the people of Israel are now oppressed and persecuted; if the person answers "I know, and I am not worthy of this," he is accepted and is taught the foundations of faith and the mitzvot. This is exactly how I was dissuaded — they were checking whether it was a passing impulse. I went through this path consciously and still want to enter the people of Israel and the covenant with the Almighty.
keyPoints: Dissuading — so that the decision is free and serious
Yevamot 47a: the question "what did you see…" and the warning about oppression
After acceptance, the candidate is taught the foundations of faith and the mitzvot
questions.explanation: The custom of dissuading is described in Yevamot 47a and in Rambam; the beit din checks the maturity of the decision.
questions.source: Yevamot 47a; Rambam, Laws of Forbidden Relations 14:1–2

questions.prompt: Who writes a Sefer Torah — the scroll for reading in the synagogue?
options: A specially trained scribe — a sofer
questions.explanation: A Sefer Torah is written by hand on parchment by a specially trained scribe — a sofer; a single error in a letter makes the scroll unfit until it is corrected.
questions.source: Lesson: The Written and Oral Torah

questions.prompt: What are the five books of Ketuvim called — Shir HaShirim, Ruth, Eicha, Kohelet, and Esther?
options: The five books of the Torah
questions.explanation: These five books are called the five megillot — "scrolls"; each of them is read on a particular day of the year.
questions.source: Lesson: The Written and Oral Torah

questions.prompt: What are the sages of the era of the Mishnah called?
questions.explanation: The sages of the era of the Mishnah are called tanaaim; the following generations, who discussed and interpreted the Mishnah, are amoraim.
questions.source: Lesson: The Written and Oral Torah

questions.prompt: Which part of the Shulchan Aruch is devoted to marriage?
questions.explanation: The Shulchan Aruch is divided into four parts. Marriage belongs to Even HaEzer; prayer, Shabbat, and the holidays — to Orach Chaim; kashrut and mourning — to Yoreh Deah; civil law — to Choshen Mishpat.
questions.source: Lesson: The Written and Oral Torah

questions.prompt: The annual cycle of Torah reading in the synagogue ends and begins again on the holiday of Simchat Torah.
questions.explanation: The Torah is divided into 54 weekly parashot; over the course of a year it is read in the synagogue in its entirety, and the cycle ends and begins again on Simchat Torah.
questions.source: Lesson: The Written and Oral Torah

questions.prompt: The Jerusalem Talmud is more extensive and authoritative than the Babylonian one.
questions.explanation: The more extensive and authoritative of the two is considered the Babylonian Talmud (Bavli); the Jerusalem Talmud (Yerushalmi) was completed earlier, around 400 CE.
questions.source: Lesson: The Written and Oral Torah

questions.prompt: What is the scroll of the Torah called that is written by hand on parchment for reading in the synagogue?
questions.explanation: A Sefer Torah is a handwritten scroll of the Torah; it is written by a trained scribe (sofer), and the annual cycle of its reading ends on Simchat Torah.
questions.source: Lesson: The Written and Oral Torah

questions.prompt: Match each megillah with the day on which it is read.
questions.explanation: The five megillot are each read on their day: Shir HaShirim on Pesach, Ruth on Shavuot, Eicha on the 9th of Av, Kohelet on Sukkot, Esther on Purim.
questions.source: Lesson: The Written and Oral Torah

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: "After the Mishnah there were further generations of teachers. Who are the amoraim, rishonim, and acharonim?" Answer.
questions.modelAnswer: The amoraim are the sages who, after the compilation of the Mishnah, discussed it in the Land of Israel and in Babylonia. Their discussions are called the Gemara; the Mishnah together with the Gemara is the Talmud. The rishonim, "the first," are halachic authorities of roughly the 11th–15th centuries, among them Rambam. The acharonim, "the later," are authorities after the Shulchan Aruch, for example Rabbi Shlomo Ganzfried, author of the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch. In this way teaching does not stop at the Mishnah, but is passed on through the generations.
keyPoints: The amoraim discussed the Mishnah; the Gemara together with the Mishnah makes up the Talmud
Rishonim — halachic authorities of roughly the 11th–15th centuries
Acharonim — authorities after the Shulchan Aruch
questions.explanation: The lesson divides the teachers into eras: the tanaaim compiled the Mishnah, the amoraim discussed it, and then come the rishonim and the acharonim.
questions.source: Lesson: The Written and Oral Torah

questions.prompt: According to the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 10:1), what does all of Israel have?
options: The land of Canaan as an inheritance
A share in the World to Come
questions.explanation: The Mishnah says: "All of Israel has a share in the World to Come" — and immediately lists those who lose it, for example those who deny that the Torah is from Heaven.
questions.source: Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1

questions.prompt: Which of the 13 principles speak about the Torah and prophecy?
questions.explanation: The principles are conveniently remembered in groups: 1–5 are about G-d, 6–9 are about prophecy and the Torah, 10–13 are about Divine providence and the future.
questions.source: Rambam, Commentary to the Mishnah, Sanhedrin ch. 10

questions.prompt: According to the lesson, which of these teachers, in the 14th–15th centuries, built a system of the foundations of faith differently from Rambam?
questions.explanation: The lesson names Rabbi Chasdai Crescas (14th–15th centuries) as the thinker who built a system of foundations differently from Rambam. Karo, Ganzfried, and Isserles are compilers of codes, not of this system.
questions.source: Lesson: Rambam's Thirteen Principles of Faith

questions.prompt: Judaism is purely a "religion of deeds": Jewish life has no worldview foundation.
questions.explanation: Judaism is often called a "religion of deeds," but Jewish life does have a worldview foundation; Rambam formulated the 13 principles as its systematic expression.
questions.source: Lesson: Rambam's Thirteen Principles of Faith

questions.prompt: Belief in the resurrection of the dead is expressed in the second blessing of the Amidah: "…You revive the dead."
questions.explanation: Techiyat haMetim — the resurrection of the dead at the end of days; belief in it is sounded in the second blessing of the Amidah.
questions.source: Lesson: Rambam's Thirteen Principles of Faith

differs.text: In the Reform siddur, the second blessing of the Amidah often has "who gives life to all" instead of "who revives the dead": the Pittsburgh Platform of 1885 renounced belief in bodily resurrection.

questions.prompt: What is the one Hebrew word for the foundations of faith (the principles)?
questions.explanation: The 13 principles are called ikarim — the "foundations" of faith; their list was composed by Rambam in his commentary to Sanhedrin ch. 10 (Perek Chelek).
questions.source: Rambam, Commentary to the Mishnah, Sanhedrin ch. 10

questions.prompt: Match the number of Rambam's principle with its content.
pairs: Unity: G-d is one, and there are no other gods
Eternity: He existed before all things and will exist forever
Prophecy: G-d reveals His will through the prophets
Immutability: this Torah will not be replaced by another
Reward for those who fulfill and punishment for those who transgress
questions.explanation: Principles 2 and 4 speak of G-d, 6 and 9 — of prophecy and the Torah, 11 — of reward and punishment.
questions.source: Rambam, Commentary to the Mishnah, Sanhedrin ch. 10

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: "Explain in your own words the first of the 13 principles — the existence of the Creator." Answer.
questions.modelAnswer: I believe that G-d exists: He created all that exists and governs all creation. For me this is not an abstract idea, but the foundation of life: the world is not accidental, it has a Creator, and I answer to Him for my deeds. In the siddur, the first text of "Ani Maamin" says precisely this: "I believe with complete faith that the Creator is the Creator and Ruler of all creations." Faith, according to Rambam, is the foundation on which a life of Torah is built.
keyPoints: G-d exists, created and governs all
Not an abstraction, but the foundation of life and responsibility
The connection between faith and a life of Torah
questions.explanation: The first principle is the existence of the Creator; the beit din expects a personal answer, not a memorized one.
questions.source: Siddur, “Ani Ma'amin,” principle 1

questions.prompt: According to Rambam, how should one treat a Jew who accepts the foundations of faith but sins out of weakness? Answer and explain.
questions.modelAnswer: Rambam wrote that one who sincerely accepts the foundations of faith enters the community of Israel, and is to be loved and treated with brotherly compassion — even if he sins out of weakness. Faith, according to Rambam, is not a set of words, but a foundation on which an entire life of Torah is built; if the foundation is there, the rest is work on oneself. That is why I treat such a person as a brother: not pushing him away and not condemning him, but supporting his return to the mitzvot. This teaches me to look at people through their faith and potential, not through their weaknesses.
keyPoints: One who accepts the foundations enters the community of Israel
He is to be loved and treated with brotherly compassion
Faith — the foundation of a life of Torah
questions.explanation: At the conclusion of Perek Chelek, Rambam speaks of love for the believer, even one who sins out of weakness.
questions.source: Rambam, Commentary to the Mishnah, Sanhedrin ch. 10

questions.prompt: When is the Shema traditionally read?
options: Only in the morning, before prayer
Only in the evening, before sleep
In the morning and in the evening
questions.explanation: The Shema is read in the morning and in the evening — "when you lie down and when you rise" (Devarim 6:7), as well as before sleep.
questions.source: Mishnah Berachot 1:1–2

questions.prompt: What sign did G-d give for the covenant with Noah and all of humanity?
questions.explanation: The covenant with Noah is the promise never again to destroy the world by a flood; the sign of this covenant is the rainbow (Bereshit 9:8–17).
questions.source: Bereshit 9:8–17

questions.prompt: In what do the sages see the special merit of the people's answer at Sinai, "naaseh ve-nishma"?
options: The people first studied all the mitzvot and only then accepted them
"We will do" was said before "we will hear" — the commitment was made before knowing the details
The people asked for a postponement in fulfilling the mitzvot
The answer was given aloud, unanimously, and sung
questions.explanation: The sages admire that "we will do" was said before "we will hear": the people took the obligation upon themselves before they knew all the details (Shemot 24:7).
questions.source: Shemot 24:7

questions.prompt: What do most halachic authorities say about women reading the Shema?
options: Women are obligated to read the Shema exactly as men are
Women are not allowed to recite the verses of the Shema at all
Women read the Shema instead of the men in the family
Women are exempt from this time-bound mitzvah, but they should at least recite the first verse
questions.explanation: Men are obligated to read the Shema at the set time; according to most authorities, women are exempt from this time-bound mitzvah, but they should at least recite the first verse and accept the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven.
questions.source: Devarim 6:7; lesson "G-d in Judaism: unity, Shema, covenant"

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, women read the Shema just as men do; the exemption from time-bound mitzvot is not applied.
In Masorti communities, women are generally encouraged to read the full Shema. The lesson notes that customs vary.

questions.prompt: The phrase "Baruch shem kevod malchuto le-olam va-ed" after the first verse of the Shema is usually said in a whisper.
questions.explanation: This phrase is not in the verse of the Torah itself. According to tradition, it was said in the Temple, and after the first verse of the Shema it is usually said in a whisper.
questions.source: Lesson: G-d in Judaism: unity, Shema, covenant

questions.prompt: Depicting G-d in human form is permitted, as long as the image is respectful.
questions.explanation: G-d is incorporeal and has no form (Devarim 4:15), therefore depicting Him is forbidden; "the hand of G-d" and similar expressions are figurative language.
questions.source: Devarim 4:15

questions.prompt: What is the act called that glorifies G-d in the eyes of people (two words)?
questions.explanation: Kiddush HaShem — the sanctification of the Name; the opposite is chillul HaShem, the desecration of the Name.
questions.source: Lesson: G-d in Judaism: unity, Shema, covenant

questions.prompt: Match the concept with its meaning.
pairs: G-d as Judge and Master of the forces of nature
The burial of texts containing holy names
Accepting the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven when reading the Shema
questions.explanation: Elohim is one of the names of G-d; texts with the holy Name are buried (genizah); chillul HaShem is the desecration of the Name; reading the Shema, the sages call the acceptance of the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven.
questions.source: Lesson: G-d in Judaism: unity, Shema, covenant

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: "The Talmud teaches imitating G-d. What does that mean in ordinary life?" Answer.
questions.modelAnswer: The Talmud (Sotah 14a) teaches imitating G-d in deeds: as He clothes the naked — so you shall clothe the naked; He visits the sick — so you shall visit the sick; He comforts the mourners — so you shall comfort them. For me this means that faith is measured not only by prayer, but also by care for people: visiting the sick, helping the needy, sharing in the joy and the sorrow of others. Such deeds are kiddush HaShem, the sanctification of G-d's Name in the world, while the opposite deeds are chillul HaShem. I strive for my life to glorify Him.
keyPoints: Sotah 14a: clothes the naked, visits the sick, comforts the mourners
Faith is measured by care for people
Kiddush HaShem and chillul HaShem
questions.explanation: Imitating G-d is one of the goals of the covenant; the beit din checks understanding through concrete deeds.
questions.source: Sotah 14a

questions.prompt: According to tradition, where did Avraham — the patriarch of the Jewish people — come from?
questions.explanation: Avraham was from Mesopotamia (Ur Kasdim, then Charan); from there G-d commanded him to go to the land that He would show him (Bereshit 12:1).
questions.source: Bereshit 12:1

questions.prompt: Who led the people of Israel after Moshe and brought them into Canaan?
questions.explanation: After Moshe, the people were led into the Land of Israel by his disciple — Yehoshua bin Nun.
questions.source: Lesson: A Brief History of the Jewish People

questions.prompt: According to the lesson, where does the word "Jew" (Yehudi) come from?
options: From the name of the king of Judea
From the name of the city Yehud
questions.explanation: The word "Jew," Yehudi, comes from the tribe of Yehudah (Judah).
questions.source: Lesson: A Brief History of the Jewish People

questions.prompt: G-d brought the people out of Egyptian slavery after the ten plagues and the splitting of the Red (Reed) Sea.
questions.explanation: This is how the lesson describes the Exodus (Shemot 12–14): the ten plagues and the splitting of the sea. This event is remembered on Pesach.
questions.source: Shemot 12–14

questions.prompt: In 722 BCE the Northern Kingdom of Israel was destroyed by Egypt, and its inhabitants were scattered.
questions.explanation: The Northern Kingdom was destroyed in 722 BCE by Assyria; after that its inhabitants were scattered.
questions.source: Lesson: A Brief History of the Jewish People

questions.prompt: What is the exile, the diaspora, called in Hebrew (one word)?
questions.explanation: For almost two thousand years most Jews lived in the diaspora — galut, "exile."
questions.source: Lesson: A Brief History of the Jewish People

questions.prompt: Match the center of Jewish life with its distinguishing feature.
pairs: The Babylonian Talmud was composed here
The "Golden Age" of poetry and philosophy
Germany, France, and later Poland, Lithuania, Russia
Descendants of the Jews of Spain and Portugal after the expulsion of 1492
questions.explanation: Great centers of Jewish life formed in the diaspora: Babylonia, Muslim Spain of the Golden Age, and also the branches of the Ashkenazim and Sephardim.
questions.source: Lesson: A Brief History of the Jewish People

questions.prompt: How did the people preserve the Torah teaching after the Romans destroyed the Second Temple? Answer as at a beit din.
questions.modelAnswer: Shortly before the fall of Jerusalem, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asked the Romans for the town of Yavneh together with its sages, and the tradition of the Torah was preserved there (Gittin 56b). Prayer replaced the sacrifices, and the center of life became the synagogue and the house of study. Later the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135 CE) was suppressed, Rabbi Akiva died a martyr's death, and Jews were forbidden to enter Jerusalem. The tradition preserved in Yavneh survived this defeat as well: the people continued to live by the Torah and prayer.
keyPoints: Yavneh and its sages, at the request of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai (Gittin 56b)
Prayer instead of sacrifices; the synagogue and the house of study
After Bar Kokhba, the tradition of the Torah was already preserved
questions.explanation: The lesson connects the survival of Judaism with Yavneh, with prayer replacing the sacrifices, and with the tradition surviving the suppression of the Bar Kokhba revolt.
questions.source: Gittin 56a–b; lesson "A Brief History of the Jewish People"

questions.prompt: What does the Aggadah's demand to see oneself "as if he himself had left Egypt" mean? Answer and explain.
questions.modelAnswer: I understand these words this way: Jewish freedom and the covenant are my personal affair, not only an event of antiquity. Every year on Pesach I must relive the Exodus as my own: I myself was a slave, and G-d Himself brought me out. This teaches me gratitude — the memory of the Exodus sounds in the kiddush, in the Shema, and in many mitzvot — and responsibility: since I am free, I am obligated to live by the Torah. For me as a ger this is especially significant: I am not a descendant of those who left Egypt, but the covenant receives me as if I myself had left.
keyPoints: The Exodus — the personal experience of every Jew
Pesach relives this memory every year
Out of gratitude — the obligation to live by the Torah
The covenant opens this memory to the ger as well
questions.explanation: The Aggadah requires reliving the Exodus as a personal event; the question checks the depth of understanding.
questions.source: Shemot 12–14; lesson "A Brief History of the Jewish People"

questions.prompt: What is a mitzvah in the exact sense of the word?
options: A good deed done by personal desire
A commandment, a command of G-d
A tradition accepted by the community
questions.explanation: A mitzvah is a commandment, a command of G-d; in everyday speech any good deed is also called a "mitzvah," but in the exact sense it is an obligation of the Torah or of the sages.
questions.source: Lesson: 613 mitzvot and the seven laws of the descendants of Noah

questions.prompt: Why does every Jew fulfill only part of the 613 mitzvot?
options: Many are bound up with the Temple, the sacrifices, the Land of Israel in the era of the Temple, the king and the Sanhedrin, or apply only to kohanim, to men, or to women
The mitzvot were cancelled after the destruction of the Temple
The mitzvot are distributed among the countries of residence
questions.explanation: Many mitzvot are bound up with the Temple, the sacrifices, the Land of Israel in the era of the Temple, the king and the Sanhedrin, and some apply only to kohanim, to men, or to women; together, the people keep the whole Torah.
questions.source: Lesson: 613 mitzvot and the seven laws of the descendants of Noah

questions.prompt: Which Hebrew letters denote the number 613, whence the expression "taryag mitzvot"?
options: The initials of the three patriarchs
questions.explanation: The number 613 is denoted in Hebrew by the letters TARYAG, which is why we say "taryag mitzvot" (Makkot 23b).
questions.source: Makkot 23b

questions.prompt: What does the law of "ever min ha-chai" among the seven laws of the descendants of Noah forbid?
options: Eating the meat of any animals
Eating flesh cut from a living animal
questions.explanation: "Ever min ha-chai" is the prohibition on eating flesh cut from a living animal; it is one of the seven laws binding on all of humanity.
questions.source: Sanhedrin 56a

questions.prompt: The blessing "…who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us…" is said only on Yom Kippur.
questions.explanation: The blessing "…who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us…" is said before the fulfillment of many mitzvot throughout the year, not only on Yom Kippur.
questions.source: Lesson: 613 mitzvot and the seven laws of the descendants of Noah

questions.prompt: In doubt about a mitzvah of the Torah one acts strictly, while in doubt about a mitzvah of the sages one acts leniently.
questions.explanation: Halacha distinguishes the stringency of laws: in doubt about a mitzvah of the Torah (de'oraita) one acts strictly, while about a mitzvah of the sages (de'rabbanan) one acts leniently.
questions.source: Lesson: 613 mitzvot and the seven laws of the descendants of Noah

differs.text: Reform Judaism does not resolve doubt by the rule "a law of the Torah — strictly, a law of the sages — leniently": ritual mitzvot are chosen by a person after study.

questions.prompt: What are the mitzvot instituted by the sages called, as distinct from the mitzvot of the Torah itself?
questions.explanation: De'oraita — mitzvot of the Torah; de'rabbanan — those instituted by the sages, for example lighting the Chanukah candles or reading the Megillat Esther.
questions.source: Lesson: 613 mitzvot and the seven laws of the descendants of Noah

questions.prompt: Match the term with its meaning.
pairs: To establish courts and just laws
The descendants of Noah, for whom the seven laws are given
questions.explanation: The mitzvot of the Torah are divided into "do" and "do not." For all of humanity, the descendants of Noah, the seven laws are obligatory; the first of them is to establish courts (dinim).
questions.source: Lesson: 613 mitzvot and the seven laws of the descendants of Noah

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: "Tell about Rabbi Akiva's 'great rule of the Torah' and about Hillel's words. How do they differ?" Answer.
questions.modelAnswer: Rabbi Akiva called the verse "Love your fellow as yourself" (Vayikra 19:18) the great rule of the Torah: it is the mitzvah to treat another with love. Hillel, answering a man who had come to convert, said it differently: "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow — this is the whole Torah, the rest is commentary; go and learn" (Shabbat 31a). This is one rule from two sides: Akiva speaks of love, Hillel — of the prohibition to do to your fellow what is hateful to you yourself. The words "go and learn" mean that ethics is the entrance into the study of the whole Torah, not a replacement for the other mitzvot.
keyPoints: Akiva: “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Vayikra 19:18)
Hillel: “What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor” (Shabbat 31a)
A positive and a prohibitive wording of one and the same rule
“Go and learn” is a gateway into studying the whole Torah, not a substitute for the mitzvot
questions.explanation: The beit din often asks about these formulations; it is important to know both the difference and the connection between them.
questions.source: Vayikra 19:18; Shabbat 31a

questions.prompt: Which events of the 18th–19th centuries led to the emergence of the movements in Judaism?
options: The emancipation of the Jews in Europe and the Haskalah, the Jewish Enlightenment
The expulsion from Spain and the founding of Sephardi communities
The destruction of the Second Temple and Yavneh
The pogroms in the Russian Empire
questions.explanation: Before emancipation and the Haskalah, Jews lived within a single traditional Judaism; the different answers to the question of how to live in the modern world became the movements.
questions.source: Lesson: The Movements of Judaism Today

questions.prompt: Who founded the Reconstructionist movement?
questions.explanation: Reconstructionism was founded by Rabbi Mordecai Kaplan (USA); it understands Judaism as the evolving civilization of the Jewish people.
questions.source: Lesson: The Movements of Judaism Today

questions.prompt: Which body makes decisions on Jewish law in Conservative (Masorti) Judaism?
options: The World Union for Progressive Judaism
The Committee on Jewish Law and Standards of the Rabbinical Assembly (CJLS)
A Sanhedrin attached to the Knesset
questions.explanation: In Masorti Judaism, halachic decisions are made by the CJLS; it allows several well-founded opinions, and the community rabbi chooses among them.
questions.source: Lesson: The Movements of Judaism Today

questions.prompt: How does Sephardi Orthodoxy differ from Ashkenazi Orthodoxy in its halachic sources?
options: It does not recognize the Oral Torah
It follows only the Talmud, without the codes
It recognizes only the rulings of the Jerusalem Talmud
It follows the Shulchan Aruch without the Rema’s glosses, plus the traditions of the Eastern communities
questions.explanation: Sephardi Orthodoxy follows the rulings of the Shulchan Aruch without the Rema’s glosses, along with the traditions of the Eastern communities; a major authority is Rav Ovadia Yosef.
questions.source: Lesson: The Movements of Judaism Today

questions.prompt: Since 1950, the Conservative movement has permitted driving to the synagogue on Shabbat.
questions.explanation: Masorti requires observing Shabbat, but a 1950 ruling permits driving to the synagogue; since 1985, JTS has ordained women as rabbis.
questions.source: Lesson: The Movements of Judaism Today

questions.prompt: Modern Orthodoxy observes more lenient laws of Shabbat and kashrut than Haredi communities.
questions.explanation: Modern Orthodox Jews observe the same laws of Shabbat, kashrut and family purity as the Haredim; the differences lie in outward appearance and in the style of participation in modern society.
questions.source: Lesson: The Movements of Judaism Today

questions.prompt: What are traditional Jews in Israel called who observe much of the tradition but do not belong to any movement (one word)?
questions.explanation: Many Israelis call themselves masortim, “traditional”: they observe a great deal but do not join any movement.
questions.source: Lesson: The Movements of Judaism Today

questions.prompt: The rabbi asks: “Explain how the movements of Judaism differ in their understanding of the Torah and of the binding force of halacha.” Answer.
questions.modelAnswer: The main difference between the movements lies in their understanding of revelation, that is, of how God gave the Torah, and, as a consequence, of how binding halacha is. Orthodoxy teaches that the Written and Oral Torah were given by God to Moshe at Sinai, and that halacha is binding today as well, although it can be applied to new circumstances through the rulings of Torah scholars. Masorti regards halacha as binding, but as a living, historically developing system; decisions are made by the CJLS. Reform Judaism sees the Torah as an inspired testimony of the people’s encounter with God, written down by human beings, and emphasizes the ethical prophetic heritage and informed personal choice. I understand these differences and am consciously choosing my community.
keyPoints: The key question is revelation and the binding force of halacha
Orthodoxy: Torah from Heaven, halacha is binding
Masorti: halacha is binding and evolving (CJLS)
Reform: an inspired heritage, informed choice
questions.explanation: The question of how one understands the Torah is central for the beit din; it is important to describe all three approaches without bias.
questions.source: Lesson: The Movements of Judaism Today

questions.prompt: An acquaintance says: “I want to do giyur, but I’ll choose the shortest path, since all conversions are the same.” What will you tell them?
questions.modelAnswer: I will say that conversions in the different movements are structured differently, and that choosing the “shortest” path is not a good idea. Orthodox giyur means accepting all the mitzvot; for a man, brit milah or hatafat dam brit; tevilah; and a beit din of three observant judges; the candidate usually lives within the community, keeping Shabbat and kashrut. This kind of giyur is recognized by all the movements. Conservative giyur also includes brit milah, tevilah and a beit din of three, and the mitzvot are accepted as Masorti understands them; it is recognized by Conservative and Reform communities. Reform giyur involves study, participation in community life, and accepting the Jewish destiny and the mitzvot through informed choice; brit milah and tevilah are not required everywhere, but many communities, including in Israel and in the CIS countries, do perform them. First it is worth understanding which understanding of the Torah and which community feel right to you, and doing giyur there, not wherever the path is shorter.
keyPoints: Conversions in the different movements are structured differently
Orthodox giyur is recognized by all the movements
Conservative giyur is recognized by Conservative and Reform communities
In Reform giyur, brit milah and tevilah are not universal, but many communities perform them
Choose a community by its understanding of the Torah, not by the shortest path
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the requirements of the three kinds of giyur and asks you to choose a movement not because “it’s easier there,” but according to your understanding of the Torah and your community.
questions.source: Lesson: The Movements of Judaism Today

questions.prompt: In which verse is it said: “The Lord, He is God; there is none besides Him”?
questions.explanation: This is Moshe’s conclusion from the unity of God seen in the Exodus (Devarim 4:35).
questions.source: Devarim 4:35

questions.prompt: What is the nature of God’s unity, according to the Rambam (Foundations of the Torah 1:7)?
options: Like that of a species: many individuals of one kind
Like that of a body: a whole made of parts and dimensions
A unity unlike any other unity in the world
A union of several “persons” in one deity
questions.explanation: The Rambam stresses that God is One and His unity is unique: not like that of a species and not like that of a body.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:7

questions.prompt: What does the principle “The Torah speaks in the language of people” mean?
options: The Torah should be read only in Hebrew
Expressions like “the hand of the Lord” are human figurative language, not a description of a body
People made up the Torah themselves
The Torah can be understood without commentaries
questions.explanation: The Rambam (Foundations of the Torah 1:9) explains that “hand,” “eyes,” “under His feet” are images adapted to human understanding.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:9

questions.prompt: According to the Rambam (Foundations of the Torah 1:11), what cannot be attributed to God?
questions.explanation: Since God has no body, bodily occurrences cannot be attributed to Him: no sides, no place, no movement; He does not change (Malachi 3:6).
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:11; Malachi 3:6

questions.prompt: What does the third of the Rambam’s 13 Principles of Faith state?
options: The Creator is not a body and has no likeness whatsoever
The Torah was passed on to people through intermediaries
Mashiach will come at the appointed time
The resurrection of the dead is the basis of reward
questions.explanation: The third principle is the incorporeality of the Creator; in the siddur it is expressed in the “Ani Maamin” formula.
questions.source: Rambam, 13 Principles of Faith; siddur, “Ani Maamin,” principle 3

questions.prompt: What is ruach hakodesh in Judaism?
options: An angel mediating between God and man
A level of prophetic inspiration that the Creator grants a person
A power a person can summon in prayer
questions.explanation: Ruach hakodesh, the “spirit of holiness,” is a level of prophetic inspiration; it is not a separate being and not a “person.”
questions.source: Lesson: One and Indivisible: Jewish Monotheism

questions.prompt: According to the Rambam, what does the beit din explain in detail to a candidate for conversion?
options: The calendar of the mitzvot and the order of performing them
The unity of God and the prohibition of avodah zarah
The history of the Jewish people from Avraham onward
The rules for pronouncing the holy Names
questions.explanation: In the Laws of Forbidden Relations 14:2, the Rambam writes that the candidate is told the foundations of the faith, the unity of God and the prohibition of avodah zarah, and that these are explained in detail.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Forbidden Relations (Issurei Bi'ah) 14:2

questions.prompt: How does Judaism regard prayer through intermediaries (angels, righteous people)?
options: It is permitted if the intermediary is righteous
It is permitted in times of trouble, but not otherwise
It is not permitted: one should pray only to God
It is permitted if God is formally addressed
questions.explanation: The Rambam’s fifth principle: one should pray only to the Creator, and not to any other being.
questions.source: Rambam, 13 Principles of Faith, principle 5

questions.prompt: In Judaism, God is One, but can be divided into “persons” or hypostases.
questions.explanation: God is indivisible: “not two, nor more than two, but One” (Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 1:7).
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:7; Devarim 6:4

questions.prompt: According to the teaching of Judaism, God can become a man or take on a human body.
questions.explanation: The Torah and the prophets teach that He has no body and no form: “for I am God, and not man” (Hoshea 11:9).
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:8; Hoshea 11:9

questions.prompt: The Orthodox, Masorti and Reform movements of Judaism all profess strict monotheism.
questions.explanation: All the movements of Judaism are united in this: none accepts the doctrine of God in three persons or of a God-man.
questions.source: Lesson: One and Indivisible: Jewish Monotheism

questions.prompt: Avodah zarah is one of the three sins that a Jew must not commit even on pain of death.
questions.explanation: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 74a) names three such sins: avodah zarah, murder and forbidden relations.
questions.source: Sanhedrin 74a

questions.prompt: Match the verse with its reference in the Tanakh.
pairs: I am the first and I am the last, and besides Me there is no God
God is not a man, that He should lie
For I am G-d, and not a man
For I, Hashem, have not changed
questions.explanation: All four verses are pillars of Jewish monotheism: God is One, not a man, unchanging.
questions.source: Yeshayahu 44:6; Bamidbar 23:19; Hoshea 11:9; Malachi 3:6

questions.prompt: Match the concept with its meaning.
pairs: “Foreign worship”: worshipping anything in place of God
Association: joining another being to the worship of the Creator
The Torah speaks in the language of people
questions.explanation: Key terms from the lesson on the unity of God; shituf is discussed within the Orthodox halachic tradition.
questions.source: Lesson: One and Indivisible: Jewish Monotheism

questions.prompt: What is “foreign worship”, the worship of anything in place of God, called? (two words)
questions.explanation: Avodah zarah is the worship of anything in place of God or “alongside Him”; it is forbidden by the Ten Commandments (Shemot 20:3–5).
questions.source: Shemot 20:3–5

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “What do you believe about God?” Answer as a candidate for giyur.
questions.modelAnswer: I believe that God is One, not two and not more than two; His unity is indivisible and unlike any other unity in the world (Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 1:7). I believe that He is incorporeal and without image: “God is not a man, that He should lie” (Bamidbar 23:19), “for I am God, and not man” (Hoshea 11:9). I pray only to Him and do not turn to intermediaries, as the Rambam’s fifth principle teaches. For me, the words of the Shema, “the Lord is One” (Devarim 6:4), are the precise formula of this faith, and I am ready to profess it with my whole life.
keyPoints: God is One and indivisible (Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 1:7)
God is incorporeal and without image (Bamidbar 23:19; Hoshea 11:9)
I pray only to Him, without intermediaries (principle 5)
A calm, clear formulation with references to sources
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the ger clearly professes the unity of God; a calm answer of a few sentences is enough.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:7; Devarim 6:4

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “You grew up in a different religious tradition. How do you now relate to your former faith and to taking part in its services?” Answer.
questions.modelAnswer: I regard my former tradition with respect: it is part of my family history, and I respect my relatives who remain in it. But my conviction is different now: I believe in the One God, indivisible, without body or image, and I do not accept the doctrine of God in three persons or the idea that God became a man. That is why I no longer take part in the services of another tradition: I cannot pray in a way that contradicts my faith. I do this calmly and without hostility toward my loved ones: it is not a rejection of people, but an acceptance of the unity of God, into which I am entering through giyur (Rambam, Laws of Forbidden Relations 14:2).
keyPoints: Respect for relatives without taking part in their services
A clear profession of the One, indivisible, incorporeal God
I do not accept the doctrine of God in three persons or of a God-man
A calm, respectful tone, without polemics
questions.explanation: A typical question for someone coming from another faith: the beit din looks at the clarity of conviction and at a respectful attitude toward relatives.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Forbidden Relations (Issurei Bi'ah) 14:2

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “In your view, can God become a man? Can a man, for example Mashiach, be God?” Answer with references.
questions.modelAnswer: No: the Torah and the prophets teach that God has no body and no form, and He does not become a man (Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 1:8; “for I am God, and not man,” Hoshea 11:9). Every human being is a creation, not the Creator, whoever he may be. According to the teaching of Judaism, Mashiach is a man, a king from the house of David, not God; a separate lesson, “Mashiach: Whom and How Judaism Awaits,” is devoted to this topic. Worshipping a human being as God is avodah zarah, one of the three prohibitions that may not be violated even on pain of death (Sanhedrin 74a), and therefore I cannot accept the idea of a God-man.
keyPoints: God is incorporeal and does not become a man (Foundations of the Torah 1:8; Hoshea 11:9)
Mashiach is a man, a king from the house of David, not God
Worshipping a human being as God is avodah zarah (Sanhedrin 74a)
An answer with references, in a calm tone
questions.explanation: This tests the ger’s readiness to clearly reject a God-man and a divine messiah, relying on the sources.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:8; Hoshea 11:9; Sanhedrin 74a

questions.prompt: In what number is the verb “bara” (“created”) in Bereshit 1:1, used with the word “Elohim”?
options: There is no verb in the verse
questions.explanation: “Elohim” is a plural of majesty; the verb used of the Almighty is in the singular.
questions.source: Bereshit 1:1

questions.prompt: Who were Avraham’s three guests in Bereshit 18, according to Jewish interpretation?
options: Angels, each with a different mission
questions.explanation: Rashi: three angels, each with his own mission; the Torah later calls them angels (Bereshit 19:1).
questions.source: Rashi on Bereshit 18:2; Bereshit 19:1

questions.prompt: If a prophet performs a sign but declares the mitzvot of the Torah abolished, he must be listened to.
questions.explanation: “You shall not listen to the words of that prophet” (Devarim 13:4); the Rambam applies this also to one who abolishes mitzvot (Foundations of the Torah 9:1–3).
questions.source: Devarim 13:2–4; Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 8:1

questions.prompt: What does the word “mashiach” (מָשִׁיחַ) literally mean?
questions.explanation: Kings and the High Priest were anointed with oil; Mashiach is the future anointed king from the house of David, a man and not a deity.
questions.source: Tanakh: the anointing of kings (Shmuel I 16:13); Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:1

questions.prompt: Who is Mashiach according to Judaism?
options: A man, a king descended from David
An angelic intermediary to whom prayer is addressed
questions.explanation: Mashiach is a man from the house of David; the Rambam writes that he will die, and after him his son and grandson will reign.
questions.source: Rambam, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin, ch. 10

questions.prompt: In which prayer, said three times a day, does a Jew ask for the “offspring of David” and the establishment of the “throne of David”?
questions.explanation: The blessing “Et Tzemach David” and the blessings for the ingathering of the exiles and the rebuilding of Jerusalem are part of the Amidah.
questions.source: Siddur, Amidah, the blessing “Et Tzemach David”

questions.prompt: What does the status “bechezkat Mashiach” say about a king, according to the Rambam (Laws of Kings 11:4)?
options: He is from the house of David, teaches Torah, strengthens it and fights the wars of G-d, but has not yet been definitively proven
He has already resurrected the dead
He has built the Temple and gathered the exiles
He has revealed a new Torah
questions.explanation: “Presumed Mashiach” is an intermediate status: the criteria concerning the person are met, but the deeds of Mashiach (the Temple, the ingathering of the exiles) are not yet complete.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 11:4

questions.prompt: According to the Rambam (12:1), what will NOT change in the days of Mashiach?
options: The established order of the world, “olam keminhago noheg”
Ignorance of G-d in the world
questions.explanation: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb” is a parable about Israel living in peace with hostile nations; according to Berachot 34b, the only difference is the end of subjugation to the kingdoms.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 12:1; Talmud, Berachot 34b

questions.prompt: How did the story of Shabtai Tzvi (1665–1666), whom thousands of Jews believed to be Mashiach, end?
options: He built the Temple in Jerusalem
He gathered all the exiles of Israel
He became king of Israel from the house of David
questions.explanation: The hope placed in Shabtai Tzvi did not pass the test of the criteria: he converted to Islam, and the Temple still does not stand.
questions.source: Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:4 (criteria)

questions.prompt: According to Shabbat 31a, what question about hope for redemption is a person asked at the heavenly court?
options: “Did you know the time of his coming?”
questions.explanation: Along with honesty in one’s dealings and time devoted to Torah, a person is asked “tzipita liyeshuah?”, “did you hope for redemption?”
questions.source: Talmud, Shabbat 31a

questions.prompt: According to the Rambam (11:3), why did it become clear that Bar Kochba was not Mashiach?
options: He was killed without completing the deeds of Mashiach
He was not descended from David
He refused to observe the Torah
The Sages demanded miracles of him, and he failed
questions.explanation: The criterion is the outcome in this world: one who is killed before completing the task is not Mashiach; the Sages did not demand signs of Bar Kochba.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 11:3

questions.prompt: What did Mashiach answer Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi when asked, “When will the master come?”
options: “Today”; Eliyahu explained: “today, if you will listen to His voice”
questions.explanation: A reference to Tehillim 95:7: “today” depends on Israel’s obedience; no exact dates are given.
questions.source: Talmud, Sanhedrin 98a; Tehillim 95:7

questions.prompt: Mashiach is a man, a king from the house of David; he is not a deity and not an intermediary to whom one prays.
questions.explanation: The Rambam: Mashiach will die, and after him his son and grandson will reign; one may pray only to the Almighty.
questions.source: Rambam, Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin, ch. 10; Laws of Kings 11:4

questions.prompt: Judaism awaits a “second coming” of Mashiach.
questions.explanation: Mashiach has never yet come, so his future coming will be the first and only one. Belief in the “return” of a Mashiach who supposedly already came is not Judaism.
questions.source: Lesson: Mashiach: Whom and How Judaism Awaits; Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:4

questions.prompt: It is forbidden to calculate the time of Mashiach’s coming: “may the bones of those who calculate the end rot away.”
questions.explanation: Sanhedrin 97b; the Rambam (12:2) repeats that no one knows how it will all unfold until it happens, and one should not calculate the end.
questions.source: Talmud, Sanhedrin 97b; Rambam, Laws of Kings 12:2

questions.prompt: To be recognized as Mashiach, a person must perform signs and resurrect the dead (Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:3).
questions.explanation: On the contrary: the Rambam writes that Mashiach does NOT need to perform signs or resurrect the dead; he is recognized by his deeds: the Temple and the ingathering of the exiles.
questions.source: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 11:3–4

questions.prompt: Match the saying with its source.
pairs: “May the bones of those who calculate the end rot away”
“Today, if you will listen to His voice”
“In its time I will hasten it”
questions.explanation: All four sayings concern awaiting Mashiach and the impermissibility of calculating the end.
questions.source: Talmud, Sanhedrin 97b; 98a; Shabbat 31a; Tehillim 95:7

questions.prompt: Match the historical figure with their role in the history of hopes for Mashiach.
pairs: Hero of the 2nd-century revolt; he fell, so he was not Mashiach
Regarded Bar Kochba as King Mashiach
1665–1666; declared himself Mashiach; converted to Islam
Asked Mashiach when he would come
questions.explanation: History knows hopes that did not pass the test of the criteria, as well as the episode of the question “When will the master come?”
questions.source: Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:3; Talmud, Sanhedrin 98a

questions.prompt: Name the king who, according to prophecy, will be the ancestor of Mashiach.
questions.explanation: Mashiach is a king from the house of David: “a shoot from the stump of Yishai,” “the offspring of David” (Yeshayahu 11:1; Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:4).
questions.source: Yeshayahu 11:1–2; Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:4

questions.prompt: What number is the “Ani Maamin” principle about the coming of Mashiach?
questions.explanation: The coming of Mashiach is the twelfth principle: “though he may tarry, I await him every day.”
questions.source: Siddur, “Ani Ma'amin,” principle 12

questions.prompt: At the beit din you are asked: “Has Mashiach come? Whom and what does Judaism await?” Answer.
questions.modelAnswer: No, Mashiach has not yet come, and I await his coming. It will be his first and only coming: there is no concept of a “second coming” in Judaism, and I do not share the belief in a Mashiach who supposedly already came and will return. Mashiach is a man, a king from the house of David, not a deity and not an intermediary to whom one prays; the Rambam writes that he will die, and after him his son and grandson will reign. He will be recognized by his deeds: he will restore the kingdom of David, build the Temple and gather the exiles, and this has not yet happened. I do not wait with folded hands: every day I say “Ani Maamin” and the blessing “Et Tzemach David” in the Amidah, and I try to live by the Torah.
keyPoints: Mashiach has not yet come; I await his coming
His coming will be the first and only one; there is no “second coming” in Judaism
Mashiach is a human being, a king from the house of David, not a deity and not an intermediary
The criteria: the Temple, the exiles gathered in; to wait = to live by the Torah
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate understands that Mashiach has not yet come and that his coming will be the first and only one.
questions.source: Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:1, 11:4; Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin, ch. 10

questions.prompt: How do you personally await Mashiach in everyday life? Answer based on the text of the lesson.
questions.modelAnswer: I await Mashiach every day — this is what the twelfth principle of “Ani Ma'amin” teaches: though he may tarry, I wait every day for him to come. Three times a day in the Amidah I say the blessing “Et tzemach David” and conclude it with the words “for Your salvation we hope all day long.” Tractate Shabbat says that at the heavenly judgment one will be asked whether one hoped for redemption, and I want to answer that not with words but with my life. For me, waiting does not mean counting the days but studying Torah, keeping the mitzvot and making the world around me kinder. At the same time, I do not calculate dates: it is said that those who calculate the end — “may their spirit expire.”
keyPoints: “Ani Maamin”: to wait for him every day, though he delays
The Amidah, the blessing “Et tzemach David,” three times a day
Hope is not passivity: living by the Torah and doing good deeds
Dates are not calculated (Sanhedrin 97b)
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that awaiting Mashiach is a daily practice of prayer and life by the Torah, not passive waiting.
questions.source: Siddur, “Ani Ma'amin,” principle 12; Amidah, “Et tzemach David”; Talmud, Shabbat 31a; Sanhedrin 97b

questions.prompt: A relative of another faith says: “Your Mashiach has already come and will come a second time.” How will you answer calmly and respectfully while remaining faithful to Judaism?
questions.modelAnswer: I will answer calmly and with respect: in Judaism, Mashiach has not yet come even once, and we await his first and only coming. The belief that he has already come and will return a second time is not Judaism, and for a Jew it is not Judaism; I respect people of other faiths, but I do not share this belief. According to Judaism, Mashiach is a human being, a king descended from David, not a deity, and he will be recognized by completed deeds: the Temple rebuilt and the exiles gathered in. Since this has not yet happened, I await his coming and am ready to explain this difference calmly at the beit din. It matters to me to remain faithful to my own tradition without belittling someone else's and without getting into arguments with people close to me.
keyPoints: A respectful tone, no arguing with relatives
Mashiach has not come; his coming will be the first and only one
Belief in a “second coming” is not Judaism
Mashiach is a human being from the house of David; the signs are the Temple and the exiles gathered in
questions.explanation: A typical situation for a giyur candidate: it is important to know the difference clearly and to answer calmly, with respect for another's faith.
questions.source: Lesson: Mashiach: Whom and How Judaism Awaits; Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:4

questions.prompt: Whom does Yeshayahu himself call the “servant” of the Almighty (Yeshayahu 49:3)?
questions.explanation: “You are My servant, Israel.” Rashi explains chapter 53 the same way: it speaks of the people.
questions.source: Yeshayahu 49:3; 41:8; Rashi on Yeshayahu 52:13

questions.prompt: To whom is the sign in Yeshayahu 7:14 addressed, according to the context of the chapter?
options: To King Achaz in his own time
To the nations at the end of days
questions.explanation: The sign is given to Achaz: before the boy grows up, the land of the two hostile kings will be deserted (Yeshayahu 7:16).
questions.source: Yeshayahu 7:10–16

questions.prompt: According to the Torah, forgiveness of sins depends on faith in the atoning death of another person.
questions.explanation: Each person answers for themselves: “the soul that sins — it shall die” (Yechezkel 18:20); the path to forgiveness is teshuvah, returning to the Almighty.
questions.source: Yechezkel 18:20; Devarim 24:16; Hoshea 14:3

questions.prompt: A teaching claims that G-d was born as a human being and lived in a body. Which of Rambam's 13 principles does it directly contradict?
options: The third: G-d has no body and no form
The seventh: on the prophecy of Moshe
The thirteenth: on the resurrection of the dead
questions.explanation: The third principle: the Creator is not a body, and the properties of a body do not apply to Him. For Judaism, belief in G-d becoming a human being is a false teaching.
questions.source: Rambam, 13 principles (3rd); Laws of Teshuvah 3:7

questions.prompt: The belief that Mashiach has already come and will return “a second time” is compatible with Rambam's 12th principle.
questions.explanation: According to the 12th principle, we await Mashiach: he has not yet come, and his coming will be the first and only one. Anything else is not Judaism.
questions.source: Rambam, 13 principles (12th); Laws of Kings 11:4

questions.prompt: Which verse of the Torah says directly that G-d is not a human being?
questions.explanation: “G-d is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should change His mind.” G-d does not become a human being.
questions.source: Bamidbar 23:19

questions.prompt: If G-d is one but consists of several “persons” or “hypostases,” this does not contradict the Shema.
questions.explanation: Rambam teaches that G-d's unity is not like the unity of a body made of parts; for Judaism, dividing G-d into “persons” is a false teaching.
questions.source: Devarim 6:4; Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 1:7; Laws of Teshuvah 3:7

questions.prompt: What does Rambam call someone who says that the Creator replaced the mitzvot of the Torah with others and that the Torah is no longer in force?
options: A prophet entitled to change the law
A righteous one among the nations
questions.explanation: Rambam counts such a person among those who deny the Torah; the mitzvot of the Torah are eternal.
questions.source: Rambam, Laws of Teshuvah 3:8; Foundations of the Torah 9:1

questions.prompt: According to the text of Yirmiyahu 31:30–32 itself, what will be written on the heart of the people?
options: New mitzvot in place of the old ones
Nothing: the mitzvot will be abolished
questions.explanation: “I will put My Torah within them and write it on their hearts” — this speaks of the very same Torah.
questions.source: Yirmiyahu 31:30–32

questions.prompt: Why does Judaism not call the Tanakh an “old,” outdated covenant?
options: The covenant of Sinai is eternal, and there is no other one replacing it
Only the five books of the Torah are called that
It is too long a name for everyday use
The Tanakh was written later than the Mishnah
questions.explanation: The Torah calls its covenant eternal (brit olam), and Rambam's ninth principle teaches that the Torah will not be replaced.
questions.source: Devarim 29:13–14; Rambam, 13 principles (9th)

questions.prompt: According to Devarim 29:13–14, the covenant at Sinai was made also with generations who were not there.
questions.explanation: Moshe says: “not with you alone… but also with those who are not here with us today.”
questions.source: Devarim 29:13–14

questions.prompt: Why is it wrong to call Reform Judaism “Orthodoxy lite”?
options: It has its own view of revelation, covenant and mitzvot, not simply a shorter list of obligations
Reform Jews are obligated to keep all 613 mitzvot but keep quiet about it
The Reform movement does not actually exist
Reform Judaism forbids prayer and Torah study
questions.explanation: It is a distinct path within the Jewish people: a different theology of obligation, not a cut-down Orthodoxy.
questions.source: Lesson “Movements in Judaism Today”

questions.prompt: Informed choice in Reform Judaism requires a person first to study the mitzvah and the voice of tradition, rather than brushing it aside for convenience.
questions.explanation: Otherwise it is not a choice but ignorance. The movement asks for a serious conversation with tradition.
questions.source: CCAR materials; lesson on the movements

questions.prompt: Which international organization unites Reform, Liberal and Progressive communities?
options: Rabbinical Assembly of the Conservative movement
questions.explanation: The WUPJ was founded in 1926; the ROOPI communities are also among its members.
questions.source: WUPJ; lesson on the movements

questions.prompt: What does the Torah promise Avraham's descendants in Bereshit 17:8?
options: A temporary right to use the land of Canaan
All the land of Canaan as an everlasting possession
Only the city of Hebron for Avraham's lifetime
Any land where Jews might wish to settle
questions.explanation: “And I will give to you and to your descendants… all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession” (Bereshit 17:8).
questions.source: Bereshit 17:8

questions.prompt: In this course, Jerusalem is called the eternal and undivided capital of the Jewish people.
questions.explanation: This is what prayer, Tehillim 137 and the history of the city's reunification in 1967 teach.
questions.source: Tehillim 137:5; lesson on the Land of Israel

questions.prompt: What does aliyah mean?
options: The fast of the Ninth of Av
Ascent, immigration to the Land of Israel
questions.explanation: Aliyah means “ascent”: moving to Eretz Israel. The Law of Return opens this path to a ger as well.
questions.source: Lesson: The Land of Israel, Zion and the State of Israel

questions.prompt: Which Jewish date is associated with the proclamation of the State of Israel?
questions.explanation: The State was proclaimed on May 14, 1948 / 5 Iyar 5708; this day is celebrated as Yom HaAtzmaut. 27 Nisan is Yom HaShoah, and 28 Iyar is Yom Yerushalayim, since 1967.
questions.source: Electronic Jewish Encyclopedia; lesson on the Land of Israel

questions.prompt: The emergence of the State of Israel cancels the awaiting of Mashiach, because the Temple is no longer needed.
questions.explanation: The people have returned to their Land, and we give thanks for this; complete redemption and the rebuilt Temple are still ahead.
questions.source: Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:1, 11:4; lesson on the Land of Israel

questions.prompt: What kind of mitzvah does Ramban see in settling the Land of Israel?
options: Merely advice from the Kabbalists of Tzfat
A Torah mitzvah for all generations
A rule in force only in the days of Mashiach
questions.explanation: Ramban, in his additions to “Sefer HaMitzvot” (positive mitzvah 4), considers settling the Land a mitzvah for all generations.
questions.source: Ramban, additions to “Sefer HaMitzvot,” positive mitzvah 4

questions.prompt: A member of the beit din asks: “What do the Land of Israel and the State of Israel mean to you?”
questions.modelAnswer: For me, it is the Land of the covenant, promised to Avraham's descendants as an everlasting possession (Bereshit 17:8). Jerusalem is the eternal and undivided capital, of which it is said: “If I forget you, O Jerusalem…”. In the Amidah I pray for the ingathering of the exiles and for the return to the city. The State of Israel, proclaimed on 5 Iyar 5708, is the return of the people to their Land, and I want to celebrate Yom HaAtzmaut as a day of thanksgiving. At the same time, complete redemption is still ahead: the Temple has not been rebuilt, and Judaism still awaits Mashiach. Love for the Land is part of my path, not a reason for giyur “for the sake of documents.”
keyPoints: The Land of the eternal covenant
Jerusalem is the eternal capital
Yom HaAtzmaut — thanksgiving for the people's return
Complete redemption is still ahead
Giyur is not for the sake of documents
questions.explanation: The judges expect a clear connection to the covenant and to the people, without reducing the answer to politics or personal gain.
questions.source: Bereshit 17:8; Tehillim 137:5; lesson on the Land of Israel

questions.prompt: Match each day with its meaning.
pairs: Independence Day, thanksgiving for the State of Israel
Remembrance of fallen soldiers and victims of terror
Mourning for the destruction of the Temples and the exile from the Land
questions.explanation: Four days are connected with the Land: two days of joy, a day of remembrance for the fallen and a day of mourning over the exile.
questions.source: Lessons on the holidays and on the Land of Israel

questions.prompt: How does Judaism teach you to read a verse of the Tanakh?
options: Pull out one phrase and pick a translation that fits a ready-made conclusion
In Hebrew, within its chapter and together with the people's tradition
Only in a retelling, without turning to the text itself
Only to those verses that confirm the new teaching
questions.explanation: A verse is read in Hebrew, in the context of its chapter and together with the tradition that has preserved the meaning of the words.
questions.source: Lesson: How to Read the Tanakh

questions.prompt: A kippah, a tallit and a Hebrew name in themselves prove that a congregation's teaching is Judaism.
questions.explanation: A teaching is recognized by what it says about G-d, about Mashiach and about the Torah, not by clothing and names.
questions.source: Lesson: How to Read the Tanakh; CCAR, 1985

questions.prompt: What does the word *almah* in Yeshayahu 7:14 mean?
options: A young woman; the sign was given to King Achaz in his time
The name of a town in Yehuda
questions.explanation: An almah is a young woman. The context of the chapter is a sign to Achaz about two hostile kings (Yeshayahu 7:16).
questions.source: Yeshayahu 7:14–16

questions.prompt: According to the Jewish reading, who is the “servant of the L-rd” in Yeshayahu 53?
options: An individual who has already come and died for the sins of the world
The people of Israel: “You are My servant, Israel”
questions.explanation: Yeshayahu 49:3 and 41:8 call the people the servant; Rashi reads this chapter the same way.

questions.prompt: What stands in Tehillim 22:17 in the Hebrew text?
options: Ka'ari — “like a lion (they maul) my hands and my feet”
A direct prophecy of the redeemer's execution
The name of the city where the Temple fell
questions.explanation: Ka'ari means “like a lion.” This is David's lament, which ends with praise in the assembly of Israel.
questions.source: Tehillim 22:17

questions.prompt: What does *adoni* mean in Tehillim 110:1?
options: The same as the Divine Name Adonai
“My lord” — a form of address to a human being
The name of the angel from Bereshit 18
questions.explanation: Adoni is the human “my lord,” not the Name Adonai. Rashi applies the psalm to Avraham.
questions.source: Tehillim 110:1; Rashi

questions.prompt: The “new covenant” in Yirmiyahu 31:30–32 abolishes the mitzvot of the Torah and transfers the covenant to another people.
questions.explanation: The prophet promises that the very same Torah will be written on the heart of Israel and Yehuda.
questions.source: Yirmiyahu 31:30–32

questions.prompt: According to Rashi, what period of time does Daniel 9 speak of?
options: The exact date of Mashiach's first and only coming
The time around the First and Second Temples
The seventy years of Daniel's life
The period after which the Torah will be abolished
questions.explanation: Rashi reads the “seventy weeks” as the span from the destruction of the First Temple through the era of the Second until its destruction.
questions.source: Daniel 9:24–27; Rashi

questions.prompt: Even a sign that comes true gives no right to abolish the mitzvot of the Torah (Devarim 13; Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 9).
questions.explanation: The Torah explicitly warns not to listen to someone who calls people away from the mitzvot, even if the sign has come true.
questions.source: Devarim 13:2–4; Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 9:1–3

questions.prompt: You are asked: “How will you tell a genuine Jewish community from a congregation that only looks Jewish?”
questions.modelAnswer: I will look not at the kippah, the tallit and the name, but at the teaching: do they speak here of one, indivisible G-d, do they await a Mashiach who has not yet come, do they regard the Torah as eternal? Before joining a new community, I will ask whether it is recognized by one of the established movements — Orthodox, Masorti or Reform — and who ordained the rabbi. If something troubles me, I will not argue on my own: I will go to my rabbi or to my beit din. Warmth and a free holiday celebration are not proof to me in themselves.
keyPoints: The teaching about G-d, Mashiach and the Torah matters more than appearances
Check recognition by the movements and the rabbi's ordination
Don't argue on your own; go to a rabbi
Kindness and a celebration do not replace checking
questions.explanation: The judges expect a calm, practical answer, not denunciation.
questions.source: Lesson: How to Read the Tanakh; CCAR, 1985

questions.prompt: Match each verse with its Jewish reading.
pairs: The servant of the L-rd is the people of Israel
The same Torah on the heart of Israel
A human leader from the line of David
questions.explanation: In all four passages, the context and the Hebrew do not support a reading about a divine redeemer who has already come.
questions.source: Lesson: How to Read the Tanakh

questions.prompt: One can live by Judaism relying only on the written text and bypassing the interpretations of the sages.
questions.explanation: Without the Oral Torah, it is unknown how to fulfill the mitzvot. The path of “only the letters, without the sages” is not Judaism.
questions.source: Lesson: The Written and Oral Torah

questions.prompt: What does Yirmiyahu promise when he speaks of a “new covenant” (31:30–32)?
options: That the Torah will be abolished and replaced by another law
That the same Torah will be written on the heart of Israel and Yehuda
That the covenant will pass to another people
That the mitzvot will remain only for the kohanim
questions.explanation: “I will put My Torah within them and write it on their hearts” — the same Torah, internalized, not abolished.
questions.source: Yirmiyahu 31:30–32

questions.prompt: How does Jewish prayer preserve the connection with the Land of Israel, even when a person lives in the diaspora?
questions.modelAnswer: Three times a day in the Amidah I turn to face Jerusalem, the eternal capital, and pray for the ingathering of the exiles and for the return to the city of David. On Pesach and on Yom Kippur we say “next year in Jerusalem.” Psalm 137 reminds us not to forget the city. Even while I live in the diaspora for now, I can study, give tzedakah, support the people in the Land and, if it works out, think about aliyah. Love for the Land does not cancel life where I am now, and it does not turn giyur into a path “for documents.”
keyPoints: The Amidah facing Jerusalem
Prayers for the ingathering of the exiles and for the city of David
L'shanah haba'ah b'Yerushalayim
Aliyah and support for the people, not giyur for the sake of documents
questions.explanation: The judges expect a concrete link between prayer, life and the Land, without reducing everything to immigration.
questions.source: Siddur, Amidah; Tehillim 137:5; lesson on the Land of Israel

questions.prompt: Why does Judaism need the Oral Torah, and what should you answer someone who suggests making do with the written lines alone?
questions.modelAnswer: The Written Torah without the Oral Torah does not explain how to fulfill the mitzvot: what counts as work on Shabbat, how tefillin are written, how shechitah is done. The sages preserved this path. To someone who says, “The lines alone are enough; the sages can be bypassed,” I will answer that this is not the path of Judaism. It is especially strange if the person meanwhile wears a kippah or lights Shabbat candles: these very customs come from the tradition of the sages. I also read the verses of the Tanakh together with the tradition, not against it.
keyPoints: Without the Oral Torah, one cannot know how to fulfill the mitzvot
The sages are part of the path, not an obstacle
Outward customs often come from the tradition of the sages themselves
Read the Tanakh together with the people who lived it
questions.explanation: This links the lesson on the two Torahs with the lesson on reading verses.
questions.source: Lessons on the Written and Oral Torah and on reading the Tanakh
